A purely psychological phenomenon unrelated to biology
A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
A social construct with no biological basis
A condition determined solely by genetics
originalOptions: A condition with a single dominant biological cause
A purely psychological phenomenon unrelated to biology
A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
A social construct with no biological basis
A condition determined solely by genetics
questions.correctAnswer: C) A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
questions.correctAnswerText: A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
questions.explanation: The biopsychosocial model frames mental illness as multifactorial, arising from the interaction of biological factors (genetics, brain function, neurotransmitters), psychological factors (personality, coping, trauma), and social factors (family, culture, employment).

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes mental health from mental illness?
options: Mental health is the complete absence of any disorder
Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
Mental illness and mental health cannot coexist
Mental health refers only to absence of psychotic symptoms
Mental health is determined by occupational performance alone
originalOptions: Mental health is the complete absence of any disorder
Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
Mental illness and mental health cannot coexist
Mental health refers only to absence of psychotic symptoms
Mental health is determined by occupational performance alone
questions.correctAnswer: B) Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
questions.correctAnswerText: Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly states mental health is not merely the absence of disease; it is a positive state encompassing emotional well-being, psychological resilience, social functioning, occupational ability, and stress coping.

questions.text: For a condition to be classified as a mental disorder, which combination of features must generally be present?
options: Disturbance in cognition or behavior, with no distress required
Any unusual thought, regardless of its effect on functioning
Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
A diagnosis made only after psychiatric hospitalization
originalOptions: Disturbance in cognition or behavior, with no distress required
Any unusual thought, regardless of its effect on functioning
Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
A diagnosis made only after psychiatric hospitalization
questions.correctAnswer: C) Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
questions.correctAnswerText: Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
questions.explanation: A mental disorder requires both a disturbance in one of the core domains (cognition, emotion, behavior, interpersonal functioning) AND that this disturbance produces significant distress or impairment affecting social life, relationships, work, or studying.

questions.text: A patient describes an anxiety symptom in which the world suddenly feels vivid, "like a rainbow," yet the sensation is distressing and overwhelming rather than pleasant. This is most consistent with which symptom?
options: Fear, with the world perceived as uniformly dark
Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
Elation, as a pure mood symptom without anxiety
originalOptions: Fear, with the world perceived as uniformly dark
Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
Elation, as a pure mood symptom without anxiety
questions.correctAnswer: B) Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
questions.correctAnswerText: Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
questions.explanation: The lecture notes panic can sometimes present as a vivid, almost euphoric perception of the world (colorful, "life feels great") rather than only the classic dark, threatening perception seen in fear, making panic recognizable in atypical presentations.

questions.text: Hallucinations and delusions are classified under which domains of the Mental Status Examination, respectively?
questions.explanation: Hallucinations (perceiving things that are not present) fall under perception, while delusions (fixed false beliefs) fall under thought content. The lecture separates these domains within the MSE, alongside thought process, cognition, insight, and judgment.

questions.text: Which of the following is emphasized as essential to always assess as part of psychiatric risk assessment?
options: Only suicide risk, addressed separately from other risks
Only substance use, as the most common comorbidity
Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
Only homicidal ideation in forensic patients
Only domestic violence in female patients
originalOptions: Only suicide risk, addressed separately from other risks
Only substance use, as the most common comorbidity
Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
Only homicidal ideation in forensic patients
Only domestic violence in female patients
questions.correctAnswer: C) Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
questions.correctAnswerText: Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
questions.explanation: Risk assessment is part of every psychiatric evaluation and must always cover this full set of areas, since each carries potentially serious and preventable consequences if missed during assessment.

questions.text: Which pairing correctly identifies the brain stimulation therapies discussed among treatment modalities?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists brain stimulation therapies as a distinct treatment modality alongside psychotherapy and medication, specifically naming ECT (Electroconvulsive Therapy) and TMS (Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation).

questions.text: According to the lecture, stigma in psychiatry manifests in three primary forms. Which set correctly represents these?
options: Structural, familial, and public stigma only
originalOptions: Structural, familial, and public stigma only
questions.correctAnswer: A) Public, self, and structural stigma
questions.explanation: Stigma manifests as public stigma (societal discrimination and stereotypes), self-stigma (internalizing negative views leading to shame), and structural stigma (institutional policies limiting rights or care), together contributing to delayed treatment and poor adherence.

questions.text: On CT, an acute intracranial hemorrhage (0–3 days old) typically appears as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Fresh blood is denser than brain parenchyma, so acute hemorrhage (0–3 days) appears hyperdense on CT. This density evolves predictably over time, becoming isodense in the subacute phase and hypodense once chronic.

questions.text: A hemorrhage older than 4 weeks (chronic stage) typically appears on CT as which of the following?
questions.explanation: As clot breaks down and fluid content increases, hemorrhage density decreases over time: hyperdense when acute, isodense when subacute, and hypodense once chronic (over 4 weeks). Confusing the acute and chronic stages is a common exam trap since the pattern is opposite to what students expect.

questions.text: Which early CT finding is characteristic of hyperacute ischemic stroke (6–24 hours)?
questions.explanation: In the early hyperacute phase of ischemia, cytotoxic edema causes cortical hypodensity with loss of grey-white matter differentiation and gyral effacement. This is an early, subtle sign, while volume loss and calcification only appear in the chronic stage.

questions.text: Vasogenic edema on brain imaging is classically seen surrounding which of the following?
questions.explanation: Vasogenic edema classically surrounds tumors, abscesses, and hemorrhages due to disruption of the blood-brain barrier. This is distinct from cytotoxic edema, which occurs in ischemia and affects both grey and white matter directly.

questions.text: Which radiological feature helps distinguish pulmonary consolidation from lobar collapse?
questions.explanation: Consolidation shows airspace opacification with air bronchograms and no volume loss or fissure displacement, since the airways remain patent. Collapse, in contrast, shows volume loss and fissure displacement toward the affected lobe, with no air bronchograms.

questions.text: Which imaging modality is preferred for diagnosing acute cholecystitis?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is the preferred modality for cholecystitis, showing a distended gallbladder, thickened wall, calculi, and pericholecystic fluid. It is also the preferred first study for bowel obstruction and appendicitis per the lecture.

questions.text: In a patient with suspected bowel perforation, which radiograph is most sensitive for detecting free intraperitoneal air?
questions.explanation: An erect chest x-ray is the most sensitive plain radiograph for detecting free intraperitoneal gas, appearing as lucent air beneath the diaphragm. Abdominal signs such as the Rigler (double wall) sign and football sign are also associated findings of pneumoperitoneum.

questions.text: A barium enema shows an "apple core" sign with eccentric wall thickening in the descending colon. This finding is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: The apple core sign reflects eccentric, annular wall thickening typical of colorectal carcinoma and is often associated with luminal obstruction. This classic contrast-study sign was specifically highlighted in the lecture for colorectal cancer.

questions.text: What is the earliest radiological finding in ankylosing spondylitis?
questions.explanation: Sacroiliitis, seen as widening or narrowing of the sacroiliac joints, is the earliest radiological finding in ankylosing spondylitis. Bamboo spine, dagger spine, and vertebral squaring are later findings that develop as the disease progresses.

questions.text: A 45-year-old woman's screening mammogram is classified as BI-RADS 4. What is the appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: BI-RADS 4 indicates a suspicious finding with roughly 2–94% probability of malignancy, so biopsy should be considered. This contrasts with BI-RADS 3 (probably benign, short-interval follow-up) and BI-RADS 1–2 (normal or benign, routine follow-up).

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the scope of urology as a specialty?
options: Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
Medical specialty limited to glomerulonephritis and interstitial nephritis
Specialty limited to female reproductive disorders
Specialty exclusively managing chronic kidney impairment
Specialty limited to prostate cancer screening
originalOptions: Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
Medical specialty limited to glomerulonephritis and interstitial nephritis
Specialty limited to female reproductive disorders
Specialty exclusively managing chronic kidney impairment
Specialty limited to prostate cancer screening
questions.correctAnswer: A) Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
questions.correctAnswerText: Surgical specialty dealing with diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract
questions.explanation: Urology is defined as the surgical specialty managing diseases of the urinary tract and male genital tract, using both medical and surgical management. Nephrology, in contrast, medically manages conditions such as chronic kidney impairment, glomerulonephritis, and interstitial nephritis.

questions.text: Regarding the vertical position of the kidneys relative to the vertebral column, which statement is correct?
options: The left kidney is 1–2 cm below the right kidney
The right kidney extends from the 1st to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
Both kidneys are at the same vertebral level
The right kidney extends from the 12th thoracic to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
The left kidney is located entirely within the pelvis
originalOptions: The left kidney is 1–2 cm below the right kidney
The right kidney extends from the 1st to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
Both kidneys are at the same vertebral level
The right kidney extends from the 12th thoracic to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
The left kidney is located entirely within the pelvis
questions.correctAnswer: B) The right kidney extends from the 1st to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
questions.correctAnswerText: The right kidney extends from the 1st to the 3rd lumbar vertebrae, and is 1–2 cm lower than the left
questions.explanation: The right kidney lies 1–2 cm lower than the left due to displacement by the liver, extending from L1–L3, while the left kidney extends from T12–L3.

questions.text: A patient with a ureteric stone is being counseled on likely sites of impaction. Which of the following is NOT a recognized site of ureteric constriction?
options: Where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels
Mid-abdominal ureter at the level of the renal pelvis
originalOptions: Where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels
Mid-abdominal ureter at the level of the renal pelvis
questions.correctAnswer: D) Mid-abdominal ureter at the level of the renal pelvis
questions.correctAnswerText: Mid-abdominal ureter at the level of the renal pelvis
questions.explanation: The three true anatomical constrictions of the ureter are the PUJ, the point where it crosses the iliac vessels, and the VUJ; these are the classic sites of stone impaction.

questions.text: During a living-donor nephrectomy, the surgical team preferentially selects one kidney for procurement based on venous anatomy. Which kidney is usually chosen, and why?
options: Right kidney, because its vein is longer
Left kidney, because its vein is longer
Right kidney, because it has more arteries
Left kidney, because it is smaller
Either kidney, since vein length is identical bilaterally
originalOptions: Right kidney, because its vein is longer
Left kidney, because its vein is longer
Right kidney, because it has more arteries
Left kidney, because it is smaller
Either kidney, since vein length is identical bilaterally
questions.correctAnswer: B) Left kidney, because its vein is longer
questions.correctAnswerText: Left kidney, because its vein is longer
questions.explanation: The right renal vein is shorter than the left, making the left kidney easier to anastomose and therefore the preferred choice in donor nephrectomy. This is a key clinically relevant anatomical asymmetry between the two renal veins.

questions.text: A 40-year-old man with acute left flank pain also reports pain radiating to his left testicle. Which of the following best explains this referred pain?
options: Direct extension of infection from kidney to testis
Lymphatic spread from kidney to testis
Shared venous drainage between kidney and testis
Common innervation of the renal pelvis and testicle via T11–T12
originalOptions: Direct extension of infection from kidney to testis
Lymphatic spread from kidney to testis
Shared venous drainage between kidney and testis
Common innervation of the renal pelvis and testicle via T11–T12
questions.correctAnswer: E) Common innervation of the renal pelvis and testicle via T11–T12
questions.correctAnswerText: Common innervation of the renal pelvis and testicle via T11–T12
questions.explanation: The renal pelvis and testicle share afferent innervation at the T11–T12 spinal levels, explaining why renal pain can be referred to the testis and vice versa. This differs from radiating pain, which spreads along a single dermatome.

questions.text: A patient presents with colicky flank pain, no fever, and is observed constantly moving and rolling in bed unable to find a comfortable position. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Ureteric obstruction from a stone
questions.explanation: Colicky, fluctuating pain with the "rolling sign" (patient unable to lie still) and absence of fever is characteristic of obstructive stone disease rather than infection. Infectious causes like pyelonephritis typically present with steady pain and fever.

questions.text: A patient describes pain that starts in the flank and is felt continuously along the same dermatome down toward the groin, without appearing in an unrelated separate site. This pattern best describes which type of pain?
questions.explanation: Radiating pain is continuous along the extent of the same dermatome, unlike referred pain, which appears in two separate sites sharing a nerve root without continuity between them. Shifting pain instead moves entirely from one region to another over time.

questions.text: A patient reports that blood is noted only at the very beginning of urination and then the urine clears. Based on the timing of hematuria, where is the likely site of bleeding?
questions.explanation: Initial hematuria, where blood appears only at the start of urination before clearing, localizes the bleeding source to the urethra. Total hematuria throughout the stream instead suggests a bladder or upper tract origin.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with gross hematuria and passage of worm-shaped (vermiform) clots. This finding most strongly suggests bleeding originating from which site?
questions.explanation: Vermiform (worm-shaped) clots form as blood is molded within the narrow ureteric lumen, indicating an upper tract source. Clot presence in general signals a more significant degree of hematuria and higher likelihood of underlying pathology.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with painless gross hematuria. What is the most common cause of gross hematuria in patients over age 50?
questions.explanation: Bladder cancer is the most common cause of gross hematuria in patients over 50 years old and must be excluded, as hematuria in adults is considered a symptom of malignancy until proven otherwise. Renal cell carcinoma is an important but less common differential.

questions.text: A patient reports waking up three times per night to urinate. How many nocturnal voids are considered clinically significant?
questions.explanation: Nocturia is defined as one or more rises from sleep to void, but it is only considered clinically significant when there are two or more episodes. Like frequency, it can result from increased urine output or decreased bladder capacity.

questions.text: A patient reports needing to use his abdominal muscles specifically during the terminal part of urination to complete voiding. This finding is best classified as which type of lower urinary tract symptom?
questions.explanation: Straining refers to the use of abdominal muscles to aid urination, normally used only at the end of voiding, and is classified as an obstructive/voiding symptom. This differs from irritative/storage symptoms such as frequency and urgency.

questions.text: A urologist is about to perform a complete physical examination on a male patient, including digital rectal examination (DRE). At what point in the examination sequence should the DRE be performed, and in what position?
options: First, in left lateral decubitus position
Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
originalOptions: First, in left lateral decubitus position
Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
questions.correctAnswer: C) Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
questions.correctAnswerText: Last, in left lateral decubitus with knee-chest position
questions.explanation: DRE should be performed at the end of the physical examination, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position with knees drawn to the chest. The examiner separates the buttocks to inspect the anus before gently inserting a lubricated finger to assess sphincter tone and palpate the prostate.

questions.text: A patient with suspected renal colic requires imaging to confirm the diagnosis. Which imaging modality is considered the gold standard for detecting urinary stones, and which modality would instead be preferred for staging prostate cancer?
options: MRI for stones; CT without contrast for prostate staging
Scrotal ultrasound for stones; bone scan for prostate staging
CT with contrast for stones; DMSA for prostate staging
CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
Renal ultrasound for stones; micturating cystourethrogram for prostate staging
originalOptions: MRI for stones; CT without contrast for prostate staging
Scrotal ultrasound for stones; bone scan for prostate staging
CT with contrast for stones; DMSA for prostate staging
CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
Renal ultrasound for stones; micturating cystourethrogram for prostate staging
questions.correctAnswer: D) CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
questions.correctAnswerText: CT without contrast for stones; MRI for prostate staging
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT is the gold standard for detecting urinary tract stones, while MRI is used for local staging of prostate cancer. Bone scan is reserved for detecting malignant prostate metastasis, not staging the primary tumor.

questions.text: On scrotal examination of an infertile male, both testes are palpable within the scrotum, but the vas deferens cannot be palpated bilaterally. This finding should raise suspicion for which underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Bilateral absence of the palpable vas deferens despite normally descended, palpable testes is classically associated with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, seen in cystic fibrosis. This is distinct from undescended testis, where the scrotum itself appears asymmetric and underdeveloped on one side.

questions.text: A 24-year-old presents with a solid, elevated skin lesion measuring 0.4 cm in diameter with no depth into the dermis. What is the most accurate term for this lesion?
questions.explanation: A papule is a solid, elevated lesion less than 0.5 cm in diameter. Nodules are larger and extend deeper into the dermis, while plaques exceed 0.5 cm and are typically formed by confluent papules. Macules are flat, not elevated, ruling that option out.

questions.text: A patient with chronic eczema who reports years of persistent scratching now has thickened skin with exaggerated skin markings over the affected area. What secondary skin change does this describe?
questions.explanation: Lichenification is thickening of the skin with accentuated markings resulting from chronic rubbing or scratching, classically seen in long-standing eczema. Atrophy describes thinning rather than thickening, making it the opposite finding.

questions.text: Skin scrapings from a scaly plaque are treated with potassium hydroxide to dissolve keratin prior to microscopic examination. This bedside test is primarily used to identify which type of infection?
questions.explanation: KOH preparation dissolves keratin to allow visualization of fungal hyphae and spores, making it the standard bedside test for suspected fungal infections. Viral infections are instead assessed with a Tzanck smear, which detects multinucleated giant cells rather than fungal elements.

questions.text: A flat, circumscribed area of discoloration measuring 0.6 cm in diameter is noted on examination, with no elevation or palpable substance. How should this lesion be classified?
questions.explanation: A macule is a flat, circumscribed discoloration less than 1 cm in diameter, fitting this 0.6 cm lesion. A patch describes the same flat morphology but only when greater than 1 cm, while papules and plaques are by definition elevated, not flat.

questions.text: What distinguishes petechiae from purpura?
options: Petechiae blanch with pressure while purpura do not
Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
Petechiae occur only on the legs while purpura occur only on the trunk
There is no size difference; they differ only in color
originalOptions: Petechiae blanch with pressure while purpura do not
Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
Petechiae occur only on the legs while purpura occur only on the trunk
There is no size difference; they differ only in color
questions.correctAnswer: C) Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
questions.correctAnswerText: Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
questions.explanation: Petechiae are pinpoint hemorrhages under 3 mm, while purpura are larger hemorrhagic lesions measuring 3–10 mm. Both are non-blanchable, distinguishing them from vasodilated erythema, but color is not the differentiating feature between the two.

questions.text: Which term describes a dried collection of serum, blood, pus, or other exudate on the surface of the skin?
questions.explanation: A crust is dried serum, blood, or purulent exudate on the skin surface, classically honey-colored in impetigo. Scale, by contrast, refers to flakes of compacted stratum corneum rather than dried fluid.

questions.text: A large, fluid-filled blister measuring more than 1 cm in diameter is called:
questions.explanation: A bulla is a fluid-filled blister exceeding 0.5 cm, while a vesicle is the corresponding smaller lesion. A pustule differs in that it contains pus rather than clear fluid.

questions.text: An elevated, plateau-like skin lesion measuring more than 1 cm in diameter is called:
questions.explanation: A plaque is a superficial, elevated, plateau-like lesion greater than 0.5 cm, often formed by the confluence of smaller papules. Nodules, in contrast, extend deeper into the dermis rather than spreading superficially.

questions.text: A transient, localized elevation of the skin caused by dermal edema, with redness that resolves within hours, is called:
questions.explanation: A wheal is a transient, compressible, edematous lesion caused by dermal edema, classically resolving within hours as in urticaria. Vesicles and bullae, by contrast, are fluid-filled and do not typically resolve so quickly.

questions.text: A solid, round, palpable lesion larger than 1 cm that extends into the dermis or deeper tissue is called:
questions.explanation: A nodule is a solid, palpable lesion extending into the dermis or deeper tissue, distinguishing it from a plaque, which remains superficial despite similar surface size. A cyst instead refers to an epithelium-lined cavity rather than a solid mass.

questions.text: Where is a patch test typically applied, and when is the reaction first assessed?
options: The thigh; assessed after 72 hours only
originalOptions: The thigh; assessed after 72 hours only
questions.correctAnswer: C) The back; assessed after 48 hours
questions.explanation: Patch testing is applied to the back under occlusion and first assessed at 48 hours, with a further reading at 72–96 hours. This delayed timeline reflects the Type IV hypersensitivity mechanism, unlike the rapid 10–15 minute readout of prick testing.

questions.text: A patient has a reddish-brown skin lesion that shows coral-pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Erythrasma characteristically produces coral-pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp, distinguishing it from pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, which instead fluoresces golden yellow. Vitiligo and pityriasis alba are pigmentary conditions rather than infections and do not produce this fluorescence pattern.

questions.text: Which is the predominant cell type in the epidermis?
questions.explanation: Keratinocytes make up 85–95% of epidermal cells, forming the stratified squamous epithelium. Fibroblasts, by contrast, are dermal rather than epidermal cells.

questions.text: Which bedside test is used to determine whether a red/purple skin lesion blanches with pressure?
questions.explanation: Diascopy involves pressing a glass slide or finger against a lesion to assess blanchability, distinguishing vasodilated erythema from hemorrhagic lesions like purpura. The Tzanck smear, in contrast, is used for cytological evaluation of vesicular or bullous lesions rather than blanching.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a secondary skin lesion?
questions.explanation: Crust is a secondary lesion that develops during disease evolution or from external factors like scratching. Papules, vesicles, nodules, and macules are all primary lesions, representing the initial reaction to a pathological process.

questions.text: The basement membrane zone primarily separates which two layers of the skin?
questions.explanation: The basement membrane zone lies between the epidermis and dermis, anchoring the two layers together. The papillary and reticular dermis are instead subdivisions within the dermis itself, not separated by the basement membrane.

questions.text: Which of the following skin lesions represents a full-thickness loss of the epidermis extending into the dermis or deeper tissue and typically heals with a scar?
questions.explanation: An ulcer involves loss of epidermis and at least part of the dermis, and therefore heals with scarring. An erosion, by contrast, is limited to the epidermis and heals without scarring.

questions.text: A lesion that is ring-shaped with central clearing is best described as:
questions.explanation: Annular describes a ring-shaped arrangement with central clearing, a pattern seen in conditions like tinea corporis. Linear and grouped arrangements instead describe lesions aligned in a row or clustered together, without central clearing.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a function of the skin?
questions.explanation: Hematopoiesis occurs in the bone marrow, not the skin, making it the exception among these options. Protection, thermoregulation, sensation, and vitamin D synthesis are all established functions of the skin.

questions.text: A patient with full decision-making capacity refuses a proposed treatment after being informed of the risks and benefits. Which ethical principle does the physician's obligation to respect this refusal reflect?
questions.explanation: Autonomy is the ethical principle granting a competent patient the right to accept or refuse medical treatment, even if that refusal may lead to a poor outcome. The physician must honor this right as long as the patient has intact decision-making capacity.

questions.text: What is the appropriate management for a patient in a "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" (CICO) situation?
questions.explanation: When intubation fails and the patient cannot be oxygenated by any other means, a surgical airway (cricothyrotomy) is the definitive life-saving intervention, bypassing the upper airway obstruction directly through the neck.

questions.text: Which term describes the situation in which healthcare providers know the right ethical care to give, but systemic constraints such as overcrowding and insurance barriers make it impossible to deliver?
options: Burnout due to excessive patient volume alone
Compassion fatigue from repeated trauma exposure
originalOptions: Burnout due to excessive patient volume alone
Compassion fatigue from repeated trauma exposure
questions.explanation: Moral injury occurs when a provider understands what ethically correct care looks like but is prevented from delivering it by external systemic barriers, distinct from general burnout or compassion fatigue, which stem from workload and emotional exhaustion rather than blocked ethical action.

questions.text: Which of the following are considered elements of informed consent?
options: Diagnosis, proposed treatment, risks/benefits, and alternatives
Diagnosis, cost of treatment, insurance status, and prognosis
Proposed treatment, physician's credentials, hospital policy, and consent form
Risks/benefits, alternatives, family opinion, and legal documentation
originalOptions: Diagnosis, proposed treatment, risks/benefits, and alternatives
Diagnosis, cost of treatment, insurance status, and prognosis
Proposed treatment, physician's credentials, hospital policy, and consent form
Risks/benefits, alternatives, family opinion, and legal documentation
questions.correctAnswer: A) Diagnosis, proposed treatment, risks/benefits, and alternatives
questions.correctAnswerText: Diagnosis, proposed treatment, risks/benefits, and alternatives
questions.explanation: Valid informed consent requires the patient to understand their diagnosis, the proposed treatment, its risks and benefits, and available alternatives (including the option of no treatment), so they can make an autonomous, informed decision.

questions.text: What is the most common ethical conflict in the Emergency Department, where the physician's desire to heal clashes with the patient's right to refuse care?
questions.explanation: This is the most frequent ethical tension in the ED: the physician's obligation to act in the patient's best interest (beneficence) conflicts with the patient's right to make their own decisions, including refusing recommended care (autonomy).

questions.text: Within how many minutes of arrival should an ECG be performed and interpreted in a patient with chest pain to detect STEMI?
questions.explanation: Current standards require an ECG to be obtained and interpreted within 10 minutes of arrival for any patient presenting with chest pain, allowing rapid identification of STEMI and timely activation of reperfusion therapy.

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS)?
options: It replaces formal radiology imaging entirely
It requires a radiologist to interpret it in real time
It is used only for cardiac indications
It allows immediate answers to binary questions, such as "Is there fluid around the heart?"
originalOptions: It replaces formal radiology imaging entirely
It requires a radiologist to interpret it in real time
It is used only for cardiac indications
It allows immediate answers to binary questions, such as "Is there fluid around the heart?"
questions.correctAnswer: D) It allows immediate answers to binary questions, such as "Is there fluid around the heart?"
questions.correctAnswerText: It allows immediate answers to binary questions, such as "Is there fluid around the heart?"
questions.explanation: POCUS is performed and interpreted directly by the emergency physician at the bedside, providing rapid answers to focused yes/no clinical questions (e.g., pericardial fluid, internal bleeding on FAST exam), which saves critical time during resuscitation.

questions.text: What is the appropriate area for patients classified as ESI Level 4 or 5 in the Emergency Department?
questions.explanation: Fast Track is designed for low-acuity ESI Level 4 and 5 patients who require zero to one resource, allowing rapid throughput for minor complaints without occupying acute care beds.

questions.text: What is the gold standard for securing a compromised airway?
questions.explanation: Endotracheal intubation, where a tube is passed through the vocal cords into the trachea using a laryngoscope, is the gold standard for securing a compromised airway, with surgical cricothyrotomy reserved as a rescue technique when intubation fails.

questions.text: A patient presents with active chest pain and suspected myocardial infarction. What is the appropriate ESI level?
questions.explanation: Active chest pain with suspected heart attack represents a high risk of deterioration or a time-critical problem, meeting criteria for ESI Level 2 (Emergent) — the patient should not wait for care.

questions.text: What is the highest priority in emergency care for a critically ill patient?
questions.explanation: Of the three pillars of emergency care (Resuscitation, Diagnosis, Disposition), resuscitation (immediate stabilization of vital signs) is the absolute highest priority, since an unstable patient must be stabilized before a definitive diagnosis or safe disposition can be pursued.

questions.text: Approximately what percentage of emergency department visits are made by patients with an AMA (against medical advice) discharge?
questions.explanation: AMA discharges account for roughly 1–2% of all ED visits. These represent high-risk legal and ethical scenarios requiring thorough documentation of the patient's capacity and understanding of the risks of leaving.

questions.text: According to EMS standards, approximately how long should it take to transport a patient with a life-threatening emergency to the hospital?
questions.explanation: The standard benchmark for EMS response to a life-threatening priority call in an urban setting is generally 8 to 9 minutes. Rapid response combined with bystander CPR significantly increases neurologically intact survival.

questions.text: A critically ill unconscious patient requires an emergency procedure, but no family member is available to provide consent. The physician proceeds because delaying treatment would threaten the patient's life. This is based on:
questions.explanation: When a patient with a life-threatening condition is unconscious or unable to communicate, the law presumes they would consent to life-saving treatment — this is known as implied consent, allowing physicians to act without delay under the "doctrine of emergency."

questions.text: Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI) generally involves the administration of:
questions.explanation: RSI involves the simultaneous administration of a sedative (e.g., etomidate) and a paralytic (e.g., rocuronium) to rapidly facilitate intubation and reduce the risk of aspiration.

questions.text: In the ABC primary survey of an unstable patient, the letter D stands for:
questions.explanation: In the ABCDE primary survey, "D" stands for Disability — a brief neurological exam (e.g., Glasgow Coma Scale, pupil response) performed to check for severe brain injury, following assessment of Airway, Breathing, and Circulation.

questions.text: Which biomarker is most specific and clinically useful for detecting myocardial injury in suspected acute coronary syndrome?
questions.explanation: Troponin is the most specific and sensitive biomarker for myocardial injury, making it the standard rapid lab test used in the ED to help rule in or rule out acute coronary syndrome in patients with chest pain.

questions.text: A 12-year-old boy has poorly controlled asthma with repeated emergency department visits. His father smokes inside the house. The physician explains asthma management and recommends that the family receive education and that all caregivers follow the medication instructions. Which principle is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Family-oriented care means the physician addresses the family structure, dynamics, and environment (such as the father's smoking) rather than treating the child in isolation. This differs from comprehensive care, which addresses multiple health domains within one patient's visit.

questions.text: A 72-year-old man with diabetes develops myocardial infarction. After hospital discharge, the family physician refers him to a cardiac rehabilitation program and arranges follow-up with the cardiologist. Which principle is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Coordination of Care involves organizing the patient's treatment and follow-up across multiple specialists and settings after a major health event. Continuity of care instead refers to an ongoing long-term relationship, not organizing referrals.

questions.text: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has been attending the same family medicine clinic every three months for the past eight years. The physician reviews his previous visits and schedules another follow-up appointment in three months. Which principle is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Continuity of Care reflects the long-term, ongoing relationship between the physician and patient built over repeated visits across years. Coordination instead refers to organizing care between multiple providers, which is not described here.

questions.text: A patient presents with uncomplicated low back pain without red-flag symptoms. The physician decides not to order unnecessary imaging, as it is unlikely to change management and may lead to unnecessary interventions. Which level of prevention is this?
questions.explanation: Quaternary prevention protects patients from unnecessary or potentially harmful medical interventions, such as avoiding imaging that would not change management. This differs from primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention, which involve actively intervening on risk factors, disease detection, or complications.

questions.text: A family physician working in a rural health center notices increasing obesity, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes in the community. After reviewing community health data, the physician organizes health education campaigns and school-based nutrition programs. Which principle is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Community-oriented care involves understanding local disease patterns and collaborating with schools and community leaders to address population-level health problems. This differs from comprehensive care, which addresses one patient's multiple health domains rather than the wider community.

questions.text: A 55-year-old man with stable angina is advised to undergo coronary angiography. After discussing the benefits and risks, he declines the procedure because he prefers medical management. The physician confirms that he understands the consequences and respects his decision. Which ethical principle is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Autonomy is demonstrated through informed refusal, where the patient understands the consequences of declining a recommended procedure and the physician respects that choice. Beneficence instead concerns acting to benefit the patient, not respecting their independent decision.

questions.text: Only one dialysis slot is available. Several patients need dialysis, so the physician prioritizes patients using transparent and fair medical criteria rather than social status or ability to pay. Which ethical principle is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Justice requires fair and equitable distribution of limited healthcare resources based on objective medical criteria rather than social or financial status. This differs from beneficence and nonmaleficence, which concern benefiting or not harming an individual patient rather than fair allocation.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with established type 2 diabetes attends follow-up. The physician counsels him about medication adherence and lifestyle changes and arranges retinal and foot examinations to prevent diabetic complications. Which level of prevention is this?
questions.explanation: Because the patient already has established diabetes, screening for complications and reinforcing adherence aims to reduce disability and further deterioration, which is tertiary prevention. This is a common exam trap since annual screening superficially resembles secondary prevention, but the underlying disease is already present.

questions.text: A family physician wants to detect diabetes at an early stage. Which of the following is an appropriate approach for an asymptomatic adult?
options: Counseling on a healthy diet to prevent diabetes
Screening for diabetes in an asymptomatic adult
Arranging annual foot examinations for a diabetic patient
originalOptions: Counseling on a healthy diet to prevent diabetes
Screening for diabetes in an asymptomatic adult
Arranging annual foot examinations for a diabetic patient
questions.correctAnswer: B) Screening for diabetes in an asymptomatic adult
questions.correctAnswerText: Screening for diabetes in an asymptomatic adult
questions.explanation: Detecting disease at an early, asymptomatic stage through screening is the defining feature of secondary prevention. Counseling on diet before disease onset instead reflects primary prevention, while foot exams in an already-diabetic patient reflect tertiary prevention.

questions.text: A 45-year-old man is a heavy smoker but has no symptoms or signs of COPD. His family physician advises him to stop smoking to reduce his risk of developing COPD and other smoking-related diseases. Which level of prevention is this?
questions.explanation: Primary prevention controls or eliminates an existing risk factor (smoking) before disease develops, as this patient has no COPD yet. This differs from tertiary prevention, where smoking cessation would instead aim to reduce complications in a patient who already has COPD.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional "4 Cs" of Family Medicine?
questions.explanation: The "4 Cs" are First Contact, Continuity, Comprehensiveness, and Coordination of Care. Curative care is not one of the four core principles, though family physicians do provide curative services as part of their broader role.

questions.text: Providing care that addresses a wide range of health problems across different conditions is known as:
questions.explanation: Comprehensiveness means addressing all aspects of a patient's health within a single encounter, not just the presenting complaint. Coordination instead refers to organizing care between multiple providers, not addressing multiple domains directly.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of patient-centered care?
questions.explanation: Patient-centered care focuses on the patient's ideas, concerns, expectations, and shared decision-making. The physician's financial interests have no place in this model and directly contradict its purpose.

questions.text: A government introduces a tax on sugary drinks to prevent obesity and diabetes before risk factors develop. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence of risk factors themselves by shaping healthy social and environmental conditions, such as taxing sugary drinks before unhealthy habits form. This differs from primary prevention, which controls risk factors that already exist.

questions.text: A patient already has an established chronic disease. Which level of prevention aims mainly to reduce complications and disability?
questions.explanation: Tertiary prevention reduces complications, disability, and mortality in patients who already have an established disease, aiming to restore function and improve quality of life. This differs from secondary prevention, which detects disease at an early, asymptomatic stage.

questions.text: Which level of prevention includes measures aimed at preventing unnecessary medical interventions, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment?
questions.explanation: Quaternary prevention identifies patients at risk of overmedicalization and protects them from unnecessary or potentially harmful interventions. This promotes evidence-based, patient-centered care while avoiding overdiagnosis and overtreatment.

questions.text: Screening an asymptomatic adult for hypertension is an example of:
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention detects disease at an early, asymptomatic stage so that prompt treatment can prevent progression or complications, as with hypertension screening. This differs from primary prevention, which would involve controlling risk factors before hypertension develops.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true regarding the historical practice of psychiatry?
options: Psychiatrists were obligated to attend executions
Early asylums lacked any legal oversight of admissions
originalOptions: Psychiatrists were obligated to attend executions
Early asylums lacked any legal oversight of admissions
questions.correctAnswer: A) Psychiatrists were obligated to attend executions
questions.correctAnswerText: Psychiatrists were obligated to attend executions
questions.explanation: There is no historical basis for psychiatrists being obligated to attend executions, making this the false statement. Involuntary institutionalization, containment-focused asylums, and insulin coma therapy are all documented historical realities of psychiatric practice.

questions.text: A patient with a history of psychotic disorder presents to the ER with sepsis. Over 10 hours, she becomes agitated, irritable, anxious, and her mental status is progressively declining. A psychiatrist is consulted. What is the first priority?
options: Protect the patient from unintended harm
originalOptions: Protect the patient from unintended harm
questions.correctAnswer: C) Protect the patient from unintended harm
questions.correctAnswerText: Protect the patient from unintended harm
questions.explanation: In an acute medical emergency with a progressively declining, fluctuating mental status, immediate safety takes priority over other steps. Capacity assessment (E) is unreliable in this unstable, evolving state, so protecting the patient from harm comes first.

questions.text: Collaboration between physical and mental health care is best supported by which of the following?
options: No interaction between physical and mental health teams
Assuming psychiatric medications have no physical side effects
Patients generally feeling more comfortable in general clinics than mental health clinics
originalOptions: No interaction between physical and mental health teams
Assuming psychiatric medications have no physical side effects
Patients generally feeling more comfortable in general clinics than mental health clinics
questions.correctAnswer: B) Easier referrals that improve outcomes
questions.explanation: Facilitated, easier referral pathways between physical and mental health services support integrated care and improve patient outcomes. Option E describes a stigma-related observation rather than a mechanism that directly drives collaboration.

questions.text: Regarding the right to die and surrogate decision-making, which of the following is FALSE?
options: The court or patient may decide
Patients have the right to refuse treatment
Surrogates must always prolong life regardless of patient wishes
If the patient has not given sufficient instructions, the state guides the decision-making process
originalOptions: The court or patient may decide
Patients have the right to refuse treatment
Surrogates must always prolong life regardless of patient wishes
If the patient has not given sufficient instructions, the state guides the decision-making process
questions.correctAnswer: C) Surrogates must always prolong life regardless of patient wishes
questions.correctAnswerText: Surrogates must always prolong life regardless of patient wishes
questions.explanation: Surrogates are meant to represent the patient's known wishes or best interests, not to mandate prolonging life unconditionally against those wishes. The other options correctly reflect accepted principles of surrogate and autonomous decision-making.

questions.text: Which ethical principle refers to proper treatment and preventing unnecessary harm?
questions.explanation: Beneficence is the duty to actively provide proper, effective treatment in the patient's best interest, going beyond simply avoiding harm (non-maleficence) to actively promoting recovery and preventing unnecessary complications.

questions.text: All of the following are irritative symptoms EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Irritative (storage) symptoms include frequency, urgency, and nocturia, reflecting bladder storage dysfunction. Intermittency is an obstructive (voiding) symptom, not irritative.

questions.text: All of the following are related to post-voiding micturition EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Postvoid dribbling, incomplete emptying, and straining occur during or right after voiding as obstructive symptoms. Nocturia is a storage/irritative symptom unrelated to the voiding phase itself.

questions.text: All of the following are signs and symptoms of testicular torsion EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A positive Prehn's sign (pain relief with testicular elevation) is characteristic of epididymitis, not torsion. Absent cremasteric reflex, high-riding testis, and transverse lie are classic torsion findings.

questions.text: Which of the following is a sign/symptom of testicular torsion?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion classically presents with sudden, severe, unilateral scrotal pain, often with nausea and vomiting — a time-sensitive emergency. Gradual pain and dysuria suggest epididymo-orchitis, while "bag of worms" describes varicocele.

questions.text: All of the following statements are correct regarding the Digital Rectal Examination (DRE) EXCEPT:
options: It is performed at the very end of the clinical examination
The patient is in lithotomy position with legs apart
The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
The prostate feels rough, hard, and asymmetrical in prostate cancer
originalOptions: It is performed at the very end of the clinical examination
The patient is in lithotomy position with legs apart
The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
The prostate feels rough, hard, and asymmetrical in prostate cancer
questions.correctAnswer: C) The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
questions.correctAnswerText: The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer classically presents on DRE as a hard, irregular, asymmetrical nodule with loss of the midline sulcus — not a smooth, symmetrical gland. DRE is done at the end of examination, typically in left lateral decubitus (not lithotomy) per the lecture.

questions.text: A patient presents with hematuria that appears only at the end of urination. Where is the most likely site of the pathology?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Bladder neck or prostatic urethra
questions.explanation: Terminal hematuria (blood at the end of urination) localizes to the bladder neck or prostatic urethra. Initial hematuria points to the urethra, while total hematuria suggests bladder or upper tract origin.

questions.text: A patient presents with flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion is a classic sign of pyelonephritis, reflecting renal capsule inflammation. Renal colic from stones causes fluctuating pain but not typically true CVA tenderness of infection.

questions.text: Which of the following is WRONG regarding scrotal examination?
options: Varicocele feels like a "bag of worms"
Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
Testicular tumor feels firm and hard
originalOptions: Varicocele feels like a "bag of worms"
Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
Testicular tumor feels firm and hard
questions.correctAnswer: B) Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
questions.correctAnswerText: Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
questions.explanation: The "bag of worms" description applies to varicocele, caused by dilated pampiniform plexus veins, not hydrocele. Hydrocele is a fluid collection that classically transilluminates.

questions.text: A patient presents with severe flank pain that radiates to the groin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Renal colic from ureteral stones causes severe, colicky flank pain radiating toward the groin as the stone travels distally along the ureter. Pyelonephritis pain is typically steady, not colicky.

questions.text: What is the normal capacity of the adult urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The adult bladder normally holds about 400–600 mL of urine. Smaller volumes are subthreshold for the urge to void, while larger volumes exceed normal physiological capacity.

questions.text: Which of the following can be detected by urinary sediment analysis?
questions.explanation: Microscopic sediment analysis identifies formed elements such as RBCs, WBCs, epithelial cells, casts, and crystals. Bilirubin, ketones, and glucose are detected chemically on dipstick, not by sediment microscopy.

questions.text: Which of the following is a common symptom of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)?
questions.explanation: Frequency is the most common urological symptom and a core component of LUTS, reflecting either polyuria or reduced bladder capacity. The other options belong to respiratory, hepatic, and GI systems respectively.

questions.text: On digital rectal examination, which finding is suspicious for prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: A hard, irregular, asymmetrical mass with loss of the midline sulcus on DRE is suspicious for prostate cancer. A smooth, symmetrically enlarged gland is more typical of BPH, and tenderness alone suggests prostatitis.

questions.text: Initial hematuria, in which blood is present only at the beginning of urination, most commonly suggests a lesion in the:
questions.explanation: Initial hematuria (blood at the start of voiding that then clears) localizes to the urethra. Total hematuria throughout the stream suggests bladder or upper tract origin.

questions.text: The upper urinary tract consists of the:
questions.explanation: The urinary tract is divided into upper (kidneys and ureters) and lower (bladder, urethra, and prostate in males) segments. This anatomical division helps localize symptoms and pathology.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a physiological narrowing of the ureter?
questions.explanation: The three physiological ureteral narrowings are the ureteropelvic junction (PUJ), the crossing of the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction (VUJ) — common sites for stone impaction. The renal calyx is not one of these constriction sites.

questions.text: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
questions.explanation: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, with each kidney containing about one million nephrons responsible for filtration and urine formation. The glomerulus and collecting duct are components of the nephron/collecting system, not the functional unit itself.

questions.text: The external urethral sphincter is composed mainly of:
questions.explanation: The external sphincter is striated muscle under voluntary control, innervated by the pudendal nerve. The internal sphincter, in contrast, is smooth muscle under involuntary sympathetic control.

questions.text: Urology is the medical specialty concerned primarily with diseases of the:
options: Urinary system and male genital system
originalOptions: Urinary system and male genital system
questions.correctAnswer: B) Urinary system and male genital system
questions.correctAnswerText: Urinary system and male genital system
questions.explanation: Urology is the surgical specialty dealing with the urinary tract (in both sexes) and the male genital tract, involving both medical and surgical management. It is distinct from nephrology, which manages medical kidney diseases.

questions.text: A patient has bone conduction better than air conduction on the right ear (negative Rinne). On Weber's test, sound is heard better in the right ear. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A negative Rinne test (bone conduction > air conduction) on the right ear indicates a conductive problem in that ear, and Weber lateralizing to the same (right) ear confirms this, since sound lateralizes toward the affected ear in conductive hearing loss. In sensorineural loss, Rinne would remain positive (air > bone) and Weber would lateralize to the opposite, better-hearing ear.

questions.text: A child presents with a midline neck lump that moves when they stick out their tongue. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A thyroglossal cyst is a midline neck lump that characteristically moves upward on tongue protrusion due to its embryological connection to the foramen cecum. Thyroid isthmus swelling moves with swallowing but not tongue protrusion, dermoid cysts are non-tender and mobile without this movement, and branchial cysts are lateral, not midline.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of referred ear pain (otalgia)?
questions.explanation: Dental disease, TMJ dysfunction, and tonsillitis are all listed causes of referred (non-otological) ear pain. A scalp lipoma is a painless subcutaneous lump, not a source of referred otalgia.

questions.text: A heavy smoker presents with hoarseness of voice persisting for 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Any smoker with hoarseness >3 weeks needs urgent fiberoptic laryngoscopy to rule out laryngeal tumor. Steroids, voice rest, or chest X-ray do not directly visualize the vocal cords and would delay this needed evaluation.

questions.text: Most common source of epistaxis:
questions.explanation: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) on the anterior nasal septum is the most common site of epistaxis due to its rich, superficial vascular anastomosis. The other arteries contribute to this plexus or supply posterior/other regions but are not individually the most common source.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of an incisional wound?
questions.explanation: Incisions/cut wounds are caused by a clean, sharp-edged object such as a knife, razor, or glass splinter/broken glass. A rock is a blunt object, so injury from it produces a laceration (irregular tear-like wound), not an incision — making it the exception among the choices.

questions.text: Smothering is best defined as which of the following?
options: Compression on neck structures by ligature
Compression on neck structures by the weight of the body
Closure of the nostrils and mouth at the same time from outside
Compression on the chest and abdomen by external force
Occlusion of the respiratory passages from inside
originalOptions: Compression on neck structures by ligature
Compression on neck structures by the weight of the body
Closure of the nostrils and mouth at the same time from outside
Compression on the chest and abdomen by external force
Occlusion of the respiratory passages from inside
questions.correctAnswer: C) Closure of the nostrils and mouth at the same time from outside
questions.correctAnswerText: Closure of the nostrils and mouth at the same time from outside
questions.explanation: Smothering occurs at the level of the mouth and nose, involving external closure of both openings simultaneously, and is mostly suicidal though it can be homicidal. This differs from gagging, which produces a similar effect but from inside the mouth (e.g., a cloth pushed into the mouth and pharynx).

questions.text: The color of skin discoloration seen in postmortem hypostasis is primarily determined by which factor?
options: The ambient temperature at the death scene
The position in which the body was found
The chemical state of hemoglobin molecules
The total blood volume remaining in the vessels
The time elapsed since cardiac arrest
originalOptions: The ambient temperature at the death scene
The position in which the body was found
The chemical state of hemoglobin molecules
The total blood volume remaining in the vessels
The time elapsed since cardiac arrest
questions.correctAnswer: C) The chemical state of hemoglobin molecules
questions.correctAnswerText: The chemical state of hemoglobin molecules
questions.explanation: Postmortem hypostasis color depends on the chemical state of hemoglobin (e.g., carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin), which is why, for example, carbon monoxide poisoning classically produces a pink or light red discoloration rather than the usual bluish-purple color. This makes hypostasis color a useful clue for suspecting certain causes of death, such as CO poisoning.

questions.text: Severity of rigor mortis is measured by:
questions.explanation: Rigor mortis develops due to falling ATP levels, causing actin and myosin to bind into a stiff gel.

questions.text: A wound that contains uneven, jagged edges is classified as:
questions.explanation: Lacerations are irregular, tear-like wounds from blunt trauma, unlike the regular, clean edges of incised wounds. Abrasions only involve superficial skin scraping, not edge irregularity, and puncture wounds weren't described this way in the lecture.

questions.text: Which of the following is a reason for urgent referral to ophthalmology?
questions.explanation: Chemical burns are true ocular emergencies requiring immediate irrigation for at least 30 minutes before any further workup, since delay risks irreversible ischemia to the eye. A, B, and D are chronic, non-urgent conditions that can be managed in routine follow-up, not urgent referral.

questions.text: The neural part of the eye is the:
questions.explanation: The retina forms the neural layer of the eye, containing photoreceptors and neurons. Cornea and sclera are part of the fibrous layer, while the lens is a refractive structure, not neural tissue.

questions.text: Which of the following is part of a routine pupil examination?
questions.explanation: Active light testing (pupillary light response) evaluates how the pupils constrict and dilate in response to light, making it the core component of a pupil examination. While slit-lamp biomicroscopy inspects the overall structure of the eye, tests like fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography (OCT) are advanced imaging techniques for the retina and blood vessels, not part of a standard pupil evaluation.

questions.text: Contact lens users are at increased risk for:
questions.explanation: Contact lens wear increases risk of microbial keratitis due to corneal surface disruption and contamination. Cataract, glaucoma, and pterygium are not specifically linked to contact lens use.

questions.text: Red eye serious symptom:
questions.explanation: Photophobia suggests corneal or intraocular involvement (e.g., keratitis, uveitis), making it a red flag symptom. Watery discharge and itching point to allergic/viral conjunctivitis, and foreign body sensation is less specific for serious pathology.

questions.text: Which radiological finding is characteristic of pneumothorax on a chest radiograph?
questions.explanation: Free air in the pleural space contains no vessels, so it appears radiolucent peripheral to the visceral pleural line. The other options belong to different pathologies (opacification/consolidation, blunting/effusion, air bronchograms/consolidation) and are not features of pneumothorax.

questions.text: Which sign on barium enema is classically associated with colorectal carcinoma? [img: apple.png ]
questions.explanation: The apple core sign reflects eccentric luminal narrowing caused by tumor infiltration of the colon wall, classically seen in colorectal carcinoma. String sign is associated with Crohn's disease, while lead-pipe and thumbprinting relate to ulcerative colitis and ischemic/edematous colitis, not colon cancer.

questions.text: Which radiological finding characterizes pleural effusion on a chest radiograph? [img: costophrenic.png]
questions.explanation: Fluid accumulation in the dependent pleural space obliterates the normally sharp costophrenic angle. Kerley B lines relate to interstitial edema, hyperlucency to pneumothorax, and tracheal deviation toward the lesion occurs in collapse, not effusion.

questions.text: Which of the following imaging modalities does NOT use ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation: MRI relies on a powerful magnetic field rather than ionizing radiation. CT, X-ray, and fluoroscopy all use x-rays, which are a form of ionizing radiation.

questions.text: Finding differentiating pulmonary consolidation from collapse:
options: Displacement of a fissure towards the opacity
Elevation of the hemidiaphragm on the affected side
Volume loss of the affected lung
originalOptions: Displacement of a fissure towards the opacity
Elevation of the hemidiaphragm on the affected side
Volume loss of the affected lung
questions.explanation: Air bronchograms indicate consolidation, where airways remain open amidst fluid-filled alveoli. Conversely, options A, B, and C are hallmark radiological signs of lung collapse caused by loss of air volume pulling surrounding structures.

allQuestions.text: Which layer of the epidermis serves as the site of origin for new keratinocytes that subsequently migrate upward through the epidermis?
allQuestions.explanation: The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer where keratinocytes proliferate before migrating upward through the spinosum, granulosum, and corneum. The other layers represent later stages of keratinocyte maturation, not sites of origin. The papillary dermis is a dermal, not epidermal, structure.

allQuestions.text: A 24-year-old presents with a solid, elevated skin lesion measuring 0.4 cm in diameter with no depth into the dermis. What is the most accurate term for this lesion?
allQuestions.explanation: A papule is a solid, elevated lesion less than 0.5 cm in diameter. Nodules are larger and extend deeper into the dermis, while plaques exceed 0.5 cm and are typically formed by confluent papules. Macules are flat, not elevated, ruling that option out.

allQuestions.text: Allergic contact dermatitis is best classified as which type of hypersensitivity reaction, and which bedside test is used to confirm it?
options: Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by prick testing
Type II hypersensitivity; confirmed by skin biopsy
Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
Type III hypersensitivity; confirmed by Tzanck smear
Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by Wood's lamp
originalOptions: Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by prick testing
Type II hypersensitivity; confirmed by skin biopsy
Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
Type III hypersensitivity; confirmed by Tzanck smear
Type I hypersensitivity; confirmed by Wood's lamp
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Type IV hypersensitivity; confirmed by patch testing
allQuestions.explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction, confirmed with patch testing where allergens are applied under occlusion for 48 hours and read later. Prick testing instead evaluates immediate (Type I) reactions such as classic allergies, making it inappropriate here.

allQuestions.text: A patient has a superficial skin lesion caused by loss of the epidermis only, which is expected to heal without scarring. What is this lesion called?
allQuestions.explanation: Erosion involves loss limited to the epidermis and heals without scarring, whereas an ulcer extends into the dermis and heals with scarring. Fissures are linear cracks rather than areas of tissue loss, and atrophy refers to thinning, not loss, of skin layers.

allQuestions.text: A patient with chronic eczema who reports years of persistent scratching now has thickened skin with exaggerated skin markings over the affected area. What secondary skin change does this describe?
allQuestions.explanation: Lichenification is thickening of the skin with accentuated markings resulting from chronic rubbing or scratching, classically seen in long-standing eczema. Atrophy describes thinning rather than thickening, making it the opposite finding.

allQuestions.text: On Wood's lamp examination in a darkened room, a depigmented patch of skin appears chalky white. This finding is most consistent with which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Vitiligo, a condition of complete depigmentation, produces a characteristic chalky white fluorescence under Wood's lamp, distinguishing it from hypopigmented conditions like pityriasis alba, which appear pale rather than chalky white. Tinea capitis and erythrasma instead produce green and coral pink fluorescence, respectively, reflecting infectious rather than pigmentary causes.

allQuestions.text: Skin scrapings from a scaly plaque are treated with potassium hydroxide to dissolve keratin prior to microscopic examination. This bedside test is primarily used to identify which type of infection?
allQuestions.explanation: KOH preparation dissolves keratin to allow visualization of fungal hyphae and spores, making it the standard bedside test for suspected fungal infections. Viral infections are instead assessed with a Tzanck smear, which detects multinucleated giant cells rather than fungal elements.

allQuestions.text: A flat, circumscribed area of discoloration measuring 0.6 cm in diameter is noted on examination, with no elevation or palpable substance. How should this lesion be classified?
allQuestions.explanation: A macule is a flat, circumscribed discoloration less than 1 cm in diameter, fitting this 0.6 cm lesion. A patch describes the same flat morphology but only when greater than 1 cm, while papules and plaques are by definition elevated, not flat.

allQuestions.text: What is the wavelength of ultraviolet light emitted by a Wood's lamp used in dermatological examination?
allQuestions.explanation: The Wood's lamp emits UVA light at approximately 365 nm, used to elicit characteristic fluorescence patterns in various infectious and pigmentary skin conditions. UVB and UVC wavelengths are not used for this purpose in standard dermatological bedside testing.

allQuestions.text: All of the following fluorescence colors on Wood's lamp examination are correctly matched with their causative condition EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Vitiligo characteristically shows a chalky white appearance under Wood's lamp due to complete depigmentation, not golden yellow fluorescence. Golden yellow fluorescence is instead the classic finding in pityriasis versicolor, an infectious rather than pigmentary condition.

allQuestions.text: What distinguishes petechiae from purpura?
options: Petechiae blanch with pressure while purpura do not
Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
Petechiae occur only on the legs while purpura occur only on the trunk
There is no size difference; they differ only in color
originalOptions: Petechiae blanch with pressure while purpura do not
Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
Petechiae occur only on the legs while purpura occur only on the trunk
There is no size difference; they differ only in color
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Petechiae are smaller (less than 3 mm) while purpura are larger (3–10 mm)
allQuestions.explanation: Petechiae are pinpoint hemorrhages under 3 mm, while purpura are larger hemorrhagic lesions measuring 3–10 mm. Both are non-blanchable, distinguishing them from vasodilated erythema, but color is not the differentiating feature between the two.

allQuestions.text: Which term describes a dried collection of serum, blood, pus, or other exudate on the surface of the skin?
allQuestions.explanation: A crust is dried serum, blood, or purulent exudate on the skin surface, classically honey-colored in impetigo. Scale, by contrast, refers to flakes of compacted stratum corneum rather than dried fluid.

allQuestions.text: A large, fluid-filled blister measuring more than 1 cm in diameter is called:
allQuestions.explanation: A bulla is a fluid-filled blister exceeding 0.5 cm, while a vesicle is the corresponding smaller lesion. A pustule differs in that it contains pus rather than clear fluid.

allQuestions.text: An elevated, plateau-like skin lesion measuring more than 1 cm in diameter is called:
allQuestions.explanation: A plaque is a superficial, elevated, plateau-like lesion greater than 0.5 cm, often formed by the confluence of smaller papules. Nodules, in contrast, extend deeper into the dermis rather than spreading superficially.

allQuestions.text: A transient, localized elevation of the skin caused by dermal edema, with redness that resolves within hours, is called:
allQuestions.explanation: A wheal is a transient, compressible, edematous lesion caused by dermal edema, classically resolving within hours as in urticaria. Vesicles and bullae, by contrast, are fluid-filled and do not typically resolve so quickly.

allQuestions.text: A solid, round, palpable lesion larger than 1 cm that extends into the dermis or deeper tissue is called:
allQuestions.explanation: A nodule is a solid, palpable lesion extending into the dermis or deeper tissue, distinguishing it from a plaque, which remains superficial despite similar surface size. A cyst instead refers to an epithelium-lined cavity rather than a solid mass.

allQuestions.text: Where is a patch test typically applied, and when is the reaction first assessed?
options: The thigh; assessed after 72 hours only
originalOptions: The thigh; assessed after 72 hours only
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The back; assessed after 48 hours
allQuestions.explanation: Patch testing is applied to the back under occlusion and first assessed at 48 hours, with a further reading at 72–96 hours. This delayed timeline reflects the Type IV hypersensitivity mechanism, unlike the rapid 10–15 minute readout of prick testing.

allQuestions.text: A patient has a reddish-brown skin lesion that shows coral-pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Erythrasma characteristically produces coral-pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp, distinguishing it from pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, which instead fluoresces golden yellow. Vitiligo and pityriasis alba are pigmentary conditions rather than infections and do not produce this fluorescence pattern.

allQuestions.text: Which is the predominant cell type in the epidermis?
allQuestions.explanation: Keratinocytes make up 85–95% of epidermal cells, forming the stratified squamous epithelium. Fibroblasts, by contrast, are dermal rather than epidermal cells.

allQuestions.text: Which bedside test is used to determine whether a red/purple skin lesion blanches with pressure?
allQuestions.explanation: Diascopy involves pressing a glass slide or finger against a lesion to assess blanchability, distinguishing vasodilated erythema from hemorrhagic lesions like purpura. The Tzanck smear, in contrast, is used for cytological evaluation of vesicular or bullous lesions rather than blanching.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is considered a secondary skin lesion?
allQuestions.explanation: Crust is a secondary lesion that develops during disease evolution or from external factors like scratching. Papules, vesicles, nodules, and macules are all primary lesions, representing the initial reaction to a pathological process.

allQuestions.text: The basement membrane zone primarily separates which two layers of the skin?
allQuestions.explanation: The basement membrane zone lies between the epidermis and dermis, anchoring the two layers together. The papillary and reticular dermis are instead subdivisions within the dermis itself, not separated by the basement membrane.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following skin lesions represents a full-thickness loss of the epidermis extending into the dermis or deeper tissue and typically heals with a scar?
allQuestions.explanation: An ulcer involves loss of epidermis and at least part of the dermis, and therefore heals with scarring. An erosion, by contrast, is limited to the epidermis and heals without scarring.

allQuestions.text: A lesion that is ring-shaped with central clearing is best described as:
