allQuestions.text: Which ethical principle refers to proper treatment and preventing unnecessary harm?
allQuestions.explanation: Beneficence is the duty to actively provide proper, effective treatment in the patient's best interest, going beyond simply avoiding harm (non-maleficence) to actively promoting recovery and preventing unnecessary complications.

allQuestions.text: Which imaging modality utilizes ionizing radiation to generate diagnostic images?
allQuestions.explanation: CT uses x-rays (ionizing radiation) to construct cross-sectional "slices" of the body, exactly like a conventional radiograph. MRI and ultrasound, in all their sequences/modes, do not use ionizing radiation, making them safer alternatives for repeated imaging.

allQuestions.text: An erect chest radiograph shows a thin white visceral pleural line with no lung markings peripheral to it, and an adjacent area that is darker than the surrounding lung. Which pathology produces this radiolucent appearance?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis with soft tissue swelling
originalOptions: Rheumatoid arthritis with soft tissue swelling
allQuestions.explanation: Pneumothorax is gas within the pleural space; because it contains no vessels or lymphatics, it appears markedly radiolucent (dark) compared to aerated lung, which still contains vascular and bronchial structures. Pleural effusion and heart failure instead produce opacity (whiteness) on chest x-ray, the opposite finding.

allQuestions.text: On a CT scan, which structures appear white?
allQuestions.explanation: CT terminology describes density relative to surrounding tissue as hyperdense (white), hypodense (black), or isodense (equal), with bone being a classic hyperdense example. "Radiolucent" is the equivalent x-ray term and "hypoechoic" is an ultrasound term, so applying them to CT is a common terminology mix-up.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best defines hydrocephalus?
options: Obstruction of CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations following subarachnoid hemorrhage
Overproduction of CSF by a choroid plexus papilloma
Obstruction of CSF flow at the foramen of Monro by a colloid cyst
Compensatory dilation of the ventricles secondary to brain atrophy
Increase in the volume of CSF causing distension of the cerebral ventricles
originalOptions: Obstruction of CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations following subarachnoid hemorrhage
Overproduction of CSF by a choroid plexus papilloma
Obstruction of CSF flow at the foramen of Monro by a colloid cyst
Compensatory dilation of the ventricles secondary to brain atrophy
Increase in the volume of CSF causing distension of the cerebral ventricles
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Increase in the volume of CSF causing distension of the cerebral ventricles
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Increase in the volume of CSF causing distension of the cerebral ventricles
allQuestions.explanation: Hydrocephalus is defined as ventriculomegaly resulting from increased CSF volume, regardless of the underlying cause. Options A, B, and C describe specific mechanisms/causes (communicating vs. non-communicating types) rather than the definition itself, while option D describes ex-vacuo ventricular enlargement from atrophy, a mimicker that is not true hydrocephalus since CSF volume is not increased.

allQuestions.text: A patient with symmetric small joint involvement shows the following radiographic finding. Which abnormality is characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis?
allQuestions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically produces marginal erosions, soft tissue swelling, juxta-articular then generalized osteoporosis, and symmetric joint space narrowing. Osteophytes, subchondral cysts, and asymmetric narrowing instead point to osteoarthritis, while sacroiliitis is the earliest radiological finding in ankylosing spondylitis.

allQuestions.text: On MRI, structures that appear white are described using which term?
allQuestions.explanation: MRI signal intensity is described as hyperintense (white), hypointense (black), or isointense (equal signal), unlike CT which uses "hyperdense/hypodense" or ultrasound which uses "hyperechoic/hypoechoic." Mixing up these modality-specific terms is a classic exam trap.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following imaging modalities relies on ionizing radiation, unlike the others listed?
allQuestions.explanation: The conventional radiograph utilizes ionizing radiation to produce images, the same principle CT is built on. Ultrasound and MRI, regardless of sequence or mode, do not use ionizing radiation, which is why they are preferred when repeated imaging or radiation avoidance is needed.

allQuestions.text: Which imaging modality avoids ionizing radiation by instead using a large, powerful magnet to generate images?
allQuestions.explanation: MRI does not use ionizing radiation; instead, the scanner consists of a large, powerful magnet in which the patient lies, and images are generated using sequences such as T1, T2, FLAIR, and DWI. CT, radiographs, fluoroscopy, and mammography all rely on x-rays.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with a new cough. What is the most appropriate initial imaging test to evaluate the chest?
allQuestions.explanation: For any chest complaint, the chest x-ray is the first study obtained, since it is fast, widely available, and gives a broad initial assessment. CT is reserved for further characterization, ultrasound is mainly used for pleural effusion follow-up or procedures, and MRI of the chest is rarely performed.

allQuestions.text: Which radiological finding is characteristic of pneumothorax on a chest radiograph?
allQuestions.explanation: Free air in the pleural space contains no vessels, so it appears radiolucent peripheral to the visceral pleural line. The other options belong to different pathologies (opacification/consolidation, blunting/effusion, air bronchograms/consolidation) and are not features of pneumothorax.

allQuestions.text: Which sign on barium enema is classically associated with colorectal carcinoma? [img: apple.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: The apple core sign reflects eccentric luminal narrowing caused by tumor infiltration of the colon wall, classically seen in colorectal carcinoma. String sign is associated with Crohn's disease, while lead-pipe and thumbprinting relate to ulcerative colitis and ischemic/edematous colitis, not colon cancer.

allQuestions.text: Which radiological finding characterizes pleural effusion on a chest radiograph? [img: costophrenic.png]
allQuestions.explanation: Fluid accumulation in the dependent pleural space obliterates the normally sharp costophrenic angle. Kerley B lines relate to interstitial edema, hyperlucency to pneumothorax, and tracheal deviation toward the lesion occurs in collapse, not effusion.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following imaging modalities does NOT use ionizing radiation?
allQuestions.explanation: MRI relies on a powerful magnetic field rather than ionizing radiation. CT, X-ray, and fluoroscopy all use x-rays, which are a form of ionizing radiation.

allQuestions.text: Finding differentiating pulmonary consolidation from collapse:
options: Displacement of a fissure towards the opacity
Elevation of the hemidiaphragm on the affected side
Volume loss of the affected lung
originalOptions: Displacement of a fissure towards the opacity
Elevation of the hemidiaphragm on the affected side
Volume loss of the affected lung
allQuestions.explanation: Air bronchograms indicate consolidation, where airways remain open amidst fluid-filled alveoli. Conversely, options A, B, and C are hallmark radiological signs of lung collapse caused by loss of air volume pulling surrounding structures.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?
allQuestions.explanation: BPH causes obstructive LUTS such as hesitancy, poor stream, straining, and incomplete emptying due to bladder outlet obstruction. Dysuria (painful urination) reflects inflammation/infection rather than mechanical obstruction, so it is not a typical BPH sign.

allQuestions.text: What is the most likely cause of continuous urinary incontinence?
allQuestions.explanation: A vesicovaginal fistula creates an abnormal communication between the bladder and vagina, causing continuous, position-independent urine leakage. Stress and urge incontinence are intermittent and related to activity or sudden urge, not constant leakage.

allQuestions.text: All of the following can cause pneumaturia EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Pneumaturia (gas in urine) results from recent catheterization, enteric fistulas communicating with the urinary tract, or infection with gas-forming organisms. An ectopic ureter causes abnormal ureteral insertion and incontinence, not gas in the urine.

allQuestions.text: Choose the conditions that cause urine to appear cloudy: (Select all that apply)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Pyuria / B) Phosphaturia / D) Chyluria
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A) Pyuria / B) Phosphaturia / D) Chyluria
allQuestions.explanation: Pyuria causes turbidity from WBCs/pus, phosphaturia from phosphate crystal precipitation in alkaline urine (classic post-meal benign cause), and chyluria from lymphatic fluid mixing with urine. If a single option is required by the question, B is selected because pyuria and chyluria change urine turbidity too, while phosphaturia remains the classic non-pathological textbook answer for cloudiness. Hematuria and bilirubinuria mainly change urine color (red/dark amber) rather than causing true cloudiness.

allQuestions.text: Hematuria can best be distinguished from hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria by which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: Dipstick testing is positive for blood in all three conditions since it detects heme, but only true hematuria shows intact RBCs on microscopic sediment analysis. Hemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria show a positive dipstick with no RBCs seen microscopically.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common cause of glomerular hematuria?
allQuestions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is the most common cause of glomerular hematuria worldwide, often presenting with episodic gross hematuria following upper respiratory infections. The other options are important but less common causes of glomerular bleeding.

allQuestions.text: What is the underlying cause of pain associated with ureteral stones?
options: Direct mechanical nerve compression by the stone
originalOptions: Direct mechanical nerve compression by the stone
allQuestions.explanation: Ureteral colic results from acute obstruction causing distension and spasm of the ureteral wall proximal to the stone, producing fluctuating, colicky pain. This differs from steady inflammatory pain, which is caused by capsular distension rather than obstruction.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are irritative symptoms EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Irritative (storage) symptoms include frequency, urgency, and nocturia, reflecting bladder storage dysfunction. Intermittency is an obstructive (voiding) symptom, not irritative.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are related to post-voiding micturition EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Postvoid dribbling, incomplete emptying, and straining occur during or right after voiding as obstructive symptoms. Nocturia is a storage/irritative symptom unrelated to the voiding phase itself.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are signs and symptoms of testicular torsion EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: A positive Prehn's sign (pain relief with testicular elevation) is characteristic of epididymitis, not torsion. Absent cremasteric reflex, high-riding testis, and transverse lie are classic torsion findings.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a sign/symptom of testicular torsion?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain
allQuestions.explanation: Testicular torsion classically presents with sudden, severe, unilateral scrotal pain, often with nausea and vomiting — a time-sensitive emergency. Gradual pain and dysuria suggest epididymo-orchitis, while "bag of worms" describes varicocele.

allQuestions.text: All of the following statements are correct regarding the Digital Rectal Examination (DRE) EXCEPT:
options: It is performed at the very end of the clinical examination
The patient is in lithotomy position with legs apart
The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
The prostate feels rough, hard, and asymmetrical in prostate cancer
originalOptions: It is performed at the very end of the clinical examination
The patient is in lithotomy position with legs apart
The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
The prostate feels rough, hard, and asymmetrical in prostate cancer
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The prostate feels smooth and symmetrical in prostate cancer
allQuestions.explanation: Prostate cancer classically presents on DRE as a hard, irregular, asymmetrical nodule with loss of the midline sulcus — not a smooth, symmetrical gland. DRE is done at the end of examination, typically in left lateral decubitus (not lithotomy) per the lecture.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with hematuria that appears only at the end of urination. Where is the most likely site of the pathology?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Bladder neck or prostatic urethra
allQuestions.explanation: Terminal hematuria (blood at the end of urination) localizes to the bladder neck or prostatic urethra. Initial hematuria points to the urethra, while total hematuria suggests bladder or upper tract origin.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion is a classic sign of pyelonephritis, reflecting renal capsule inflammation. Renal colic from stones causes fluctuating pain but not typically true CVA tenderness of infection.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is WRONG regarding scrotal examination?
options: Varicocele feels like a "bag of worms"
Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
Testicular tumor feels firm and hard
originalOptions: Varicocele feels like a "bag of worms"
Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
Testicular tumor feels firm and hard
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Hydrocele is described as a "bag of worms"
allQuestions.explanation: The "bag of worms" description applies to varicocele, caused by dilated pampiniform plexus veins, not hydrocele. Hydrocele is a fluid collection that classically transilluminates.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with severe flank pain that radiates to the groin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Renal colic from ureteral stones causes severe, colicky flank pain radiating toward the groin as the stone travels distally along the ureter. Pyelonephritis pain is typically steady, not colicky.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following questions should be asked in a patient presenting with hematuria?
options: Is there pain associated with the hematuria?
Is there a history of dysuria, frequency, or urgency?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure?
Is there a history of trauma or recent instrumentation?
originalOptions: Is there pain associated with the hematuria?
Is there a history of dysuria, frequency, or urgency?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure?
Is there a history of trauma or recent instrumentation?
allQuestions.explanation: A thorough hematuria history should assess pain, associated LUTS, and risk factors such as smoking, occupational carcinogen exposure, and recent trauma or instrumentation. Each of these helps localize the cause and assess malignancy risk.

allQuestions.text: What is the normal capacity of the adult urinary bladder?
allQuestions.explanation: The adult bladder normally holds about 400–600 mL of urine. Smaller volumes are subthreshold for the urge to void, while larger volumes exceed normal physiological capacity.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following can be detected by urinary sediment analysis?
allQuestions.explanation: Microscopic sediment analysis identifies formed elements such as RBCs, WBCs, epithelial cells, casts, and crystals. Bilirubin, ketones, and glucose are detected chemically on dipstick, not by sediment microscopy.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a common symptom of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)?
allQuestions.explanation: Frequency is the most common urological symptom and a core component of LUTS, reflecting either polyuria or reduced bladder capacity. The other options belong to respiratory, hepatic, and GI systems respectively.

allQuestions.text: On digital rectal examination, which finding is suspicious for prostate cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: A hard, irregular, asymmetrical mass with loss of the midline sulcus on DRE is suspicious for prostate cancer. A smooth, symmetrically enlarged gland is more typical of BPH, and tenderness alone suggests prostatitis.

allQuestions.text: Initial hematuria, in which blood is present only at the beginning of urination, most commonly suggests a lesion in the:
allQuestions.explanation: Initial hematuria (blood at the start of voiding that then clears) localizes to the urethra. Total hematuria throughout the stream suggests bladder or upper tract origin.

allQuestions.text: The upper urinary tract consists of the:
allQuestions.explanation: The urinary tract is divided into upper (kidneys and ureters) and lower (bladder, urethra, and prostate in males) segments. This anatomical division helps localize symptoms and pathology.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a physiological narrowing of the ureter?
allQuestions.explanation: The three physiological ureteral narrowings are the ureteropelvic junction (PUJ), the crossing of the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction (VUJ) — common sites for stone impaction. The renal calyx is not one of these constriction sites.

allQuestions.text: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
allQuestions.explanation: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, with each kidney containing about one million nephrons responsible for filtration and urine formation. The glomerulus and collecting duct are components of the nephron/collecting system, not the functional unit itself.

allQuestions.text: The external urethral sphincter is composed mainly of:
allQuestions.explanation: The external sphincter is striated muscle under voluntary control, innervated by the pudendal nerve. The internal sphincter, in contrast, is smooth muscle under involuntary sympathetic control.

allQuestions.text: Urology is the medical specialty concerned primarily with diseases of the:
options: Urinary system and male genital system
originalOptions: Urinary system and male genital system
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Urinary system and male genital system
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Urinary system and male genital system
allQuestions.explanation: Urology is the surgical specialty dealing with the urinary tract (in both sexes) and the male genital tract, involving both medical and surgical management. It is distinct from nephrology, which manages medical kidney diseases.

allQuestions.text: A Tzanck smear performed on scrapings from the base of a vesicle reveals multinucleated giant cells. This finding is most consistent with which infection?
allQuestions.explanation: Multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear are the classic finding in herpes simplex and varicella zoster infections. Acantholytic cells, not multinucleated giant cells, are the characteristic finding in pemphigus.

allQuestions.text: Which investigation involves introducing allergen into the skin and assessing for a wheal-and-flare reaction within 10-15 minutes?
allQuestions.explanation: Prick testing evaluates immediate Type I hypersensitivity by introducing allergen into the skin and observing wheal formation within 10-15 minutes. Patch testing instead assesses delayed Type IV reactions over 48 hours.

allQuestions.text: Which dermal cell type is primarily responsible for synthesizing collagen, elastin, and other extracellular matrix components?
allQuestions.explanation: Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, elastin, glycosaminoglycans, and other extracellular matrix components that give the dermis its structural support. Mast cells and macrophages instead contribute to inflammatory and immune functions.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with pinpoint, non-blanchable hemorrhagic lesions measuring less than 3 mm in diameter. What is the appropriate term for these lesions?
allQuestions.explanation: Petechiae are pinpoint, non-blanchable hemorrhages less than 3 mm, often indicating platelet abnormalities or vasculopathy. Purpura and ecchymosis describe larger hemorrhagic lesions, 3-10 mm and greater than 10 mm respectively.

allQuestions.text: Which clinical sign, characterized by pinpoint bleeding upon removal of overlying scale, is classically associated with a papulosquamous condition featuring well-defined plaques on extensor surfaces?
allQuestions.explanation: The Auspitz sign, pinpoint bleeding after scale removal, is a special feature of psoriasis, which presents with well-defined, silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces. Wickham's striae instead refer to fine white lines seen in lichen planus.

allQuestions.text: Purple, polygonal, pruritic papules and plaques with fine white lines on their surface, commonly affecting the wrists and oral mucosa, are associated with which named surface finding?
allQuestions.explanation: Wickham's striae are fine white lines seen on the surface of lichen planus papules, a helpful diagnostic feature alongside the classic purple, polygonal, pruritic morphology. The Auspitz sign, by contrast, is specific to psoriasis rather than lichen planus.

allQuestions.text: A generalized papulosquamous eruption preceded by a single larger lesion, followed by a distribution along skin lines on the trunk, is most consistent with which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Pityriasis rosea characteristically begins with a herald patch followed by a generalized eruption oriented along skin lines, producing a "Christmas tree" pattern on the trunk. Psoriasis instead favors extensor surfaces with well-defined, silvery plaques rather than a herald patch.

allQuestions.text: A red lesion does not fade when compressed with a glass slide. This negative diascopy result is most consistent with which underlying process?
allQuestions.explanation: Non-blanchable redness on diascopy indicates hemorrhage with extravasated blood outside the vasculature, as seen in purpura or petechiae. Blanchable lesions such as urticaria and telangiectasia result from vasodilation rather than hemorrhage.

allQuestions.text: Patch testing for suspected allergic contact dermatitis involves applying allergens under occlusion to the skin for how long before the initial reading?
allQuestions.explanation: Patch testing requires allergens to remain under occlusion on the skin for 48 hours, with reactions reassessed later at 72-96 hours. This delayed timeline reflects the Type IV hypersensitivity mechanism being tested, unlike the rapid 10-15 minute readout of prick testing.

allQuestions.text: Which epidermal layer is composed mainly of lipids and functions as the primary barrier preventing penetration of harmful substances and moisture loss
allQuestions.explanation: The stratum corneum is the outermost, dead, lipid-rich layer that serves as the skin's principal barrier against harmful substances and moisture loss. The stratum basale, by contrast, is the deepest proliferative layer rather than the barrier layer.

allQuestions.text: Damage to desmosomal connections between keratinocytes, as seen in pemphigus, results in which histological finding?
allQuestions.explanation: Desmosomes maintain keratinocyte adhesion, and their disruption produces acantholysis, the loss of cell-to-cell cohesion characteristic of pemphigus. This differs from hyperkeratosis, which reflects excess stratum corneum thickening rather than loss of adhesion.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with red, non-blanchable, palpable lesions on the legs that are painful and have persisted for several weeks. Which condition is most likely?
allQuestions.explanation: Vasculitis classically presents as palpable, non-blanchable purpura on the legs, often painful and persisting for weeks, reflecting a hemorrhagic rather than vasodilatory process. Urticaria, in contrast, is blanchable and transient, resolving within hours.

allQuestions.text: A skin defect extending through the epidermis and into at least part of the dermis, expected to heal with scar formation, is best classified as which lesion?
allQuestions.explanation: An ulcer involves loss of epidermis and at least part of the dermis, and therefore heals with scarring. An erosion is limited to the epidermis alone and heals without scarring, distinguishing it from an ulcer.

allQuestions.text: Which feature most reliably distinguishes eczema from psoriasis on clinical examination?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Ill-defined margins versus well-defined margins
allQuestions.explanation: Eczema classically has ill-defined margins, whereas psoriasis presents with sharply well-defined plaque margins, making margin definition a key distinguishing feature. Scale, erythema, and pruritus can occur in both conditions and are therefore less discriminating.

allQuestions.text: Linear, curvilinear tracks in the epidermis produced by a burrowing organism are known as which special skin lesion, and are diagnostic of which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Burrows are linear or curvilinear tracts created by burrowing mites and are diagnostic for scabies infestation. Fissures, by contrast, are linear cracks caused by mechanical splitting rather than parasitic burrowing.

allQuestions.text: Which ossicle's footplate is attached directly to the oval window, transmitting sound into the inner ear?
allQuestions.explanation: The stapes footplate sits on the oval window and pushes on it to generate perilymph waves in the cochlea, continuing the sound conduction pathway. The malleus and incus are earlier links in the ossicular chain but do not directly contact the oval window.

allQuestions.text: A 70-year-old poorly controlled diabetic presents with severe otalgia and granulation tissue in the ear canal. Which diagnosis must be suspected?
allQuestions.explanation: Severe otalgia in an elderly patient with uncontrolled diabetes is a classic red flag for necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa, an aggressive infection that can extend to the skull base. Acute otitis externa and media are far more common but do not carry this specific risk profile of severe pain plus uncontrolled diabetes.

allQuestions.text: Shedding of otoconia (crystals) from the utricle into the semicircular canals is the underlying mechanism of which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: BPPV results from displaced otoconia (crystals) from the utricle entering the semicircular canals, causing brief seconds-long vertigo with position change. Ménière's disease involves endolymphatic hydrops instead, and vestibular neuritis is due to inflammation, not crystal displacement.

allQuestions.text: A patient reports recurrent vertigo lasting hours, associated with fluctuating unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: The triad of episodic vertigo (hours), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness is characteristic of Ménière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops). BPPV lasts seconds and vestibular neuritis lasts days, and neither is typically associated with hearing loss.

allQuestions.text: Vesicles in the ear canal accompanied by ipsilateral facial nerve palsy should raise suspicion for which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) presents with vesicles in the ear canal, facial nerve palsy, and sometimes vertigo or sensorineural hearing loss. This combination of vesicles plus facial palsy is not typical of the other otological conditions listed.

allQuestions.text: On Weber's test, sound lateralizes to the right ear. Rinne's test on the right shows bone conduction greater than air conduction. What is the diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Lateralization to the affected ear on Weber's test combined with a negative Rinne's test (bone conduction greater than air conduction) on that same side confirms a conductive hearing loss in the right ear. Sensorineural loss would instead lateralize away from the affected ear with a positive Rinne's test.

allQuestions.text: What is the primary function of the Eustachian tube?
options: Transmission of vibration to the cochlea
Ventilation and equalization of middle ear pressure
originalOptions: Transmission of vibration to the cochlea
Ventilation and equalization of middle ear pressure
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Ventilation and equalization of middle ear pressure
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Ventilation and equalization of middle ear pressure
allQuestions.explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and functions to ventilate the middle ear space, equalizing its pressure with atmospheric pressure. Sound amplification and vibration transmission are functions of the ossicles, not the Eustachian tube.

allQuestions.text: During an emergency airway obstruction, a cricothyrotomy is performed through which structure?
allQuestions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane, located between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, is the site used for emergency cricothyrotomy due to its superficial and relatively avascular location. The cricoid cartilage and thyroid isthmus are nearby structures but are not the incision site for this procedure.

allQuestions.text: A 55-year-old smoker presents with hoarseness of voice persisting for more than 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start proton pump inhibitor and observe
Voice rest and follow-up in 1 month
Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
originalOptions: Start proton pump inhibitor and observe
Voice rest and follow-up in 1 month
Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Urgent referral to ENT for fiberoptic laryngoscopy
allQuestions.explanation: Persistent hoarseness beyond 3 weeks in a smoker is a red flag for laryngeal malignancy and warrants urgent ENT referral for fiberoptic endoscopy to visualize the vocal cords and rule out tumors. Reassurance, antibiotics, or symptomatic measures risk delaying diagnosis of a potentially neoplastic process.

allQuestions.text: Tenderness elicited on palpation of the tragus is most suggestive of which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: Tragal tenderness on palpation is a classic clinical sign of otitis externa, as inflammation of the external auditory canal makes movement of the pinna/tragus painful. Acute otitis media, a middle ear condition, does not typically produce tragal tenderness since the external ear is not primarily inflamed.

allQuestions.text: Which level of prehospital care provider is trained to perform endotracheal intubation, establish IV access, and administer a wide range of emergency medications?
allQuestions.explanation: Paramedics provide Advanced Life Support (ALS), including intubation, IV access, cardiac monitoring, and administration of emergency drugs. EMRs and EMTs are limited to basic interventions like CPR, bleeding control, and non-invasive airway management. Critical Care Transport teams handle complex inter-facility transfers, not initial field ALS care.

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives unresponsive with severe respiratory distress and profound shock. According to the Emergency Severity Index, which triage level should this patient receive?
allQuestions.explanation: ESI Level 1 is reserved for patients requiring immediate, life-saving intervention without delay, such as those in profound shock or unresponsive with severe respiratory distress.

allQuestions.text: During the primary trauma survey, which step involves controlling external hemorrhage and establishing large-bore IV access?
allQuestions.explanation: The "C" in the ABCs of trauma resuscitation stands for Circulation, which includes assessing pulses, controlling external bleeding, and obtaining IV access for fluids or blood. Airway and Breathing precede Circulation, while Disability refers to the neurological exam. Bleeding must be controlled before resuscitation can proceed effectively.

allQuestions.text: An unconscious trauma patient arrives in the ED with no family present. Under which legal doctrine can the emergency physician proceed with life-saving treatment without formal consent?
allQuestions.explanation: The Implied consent (Doctrine of Emergency) presumes that an unconscious patient with a life-threatening condition would consent to life-saving treatment, allowing physicians to act without formal consent. Informed consent requires an awake, capable patient to explicitly agree. Advance directives and guardianship require pre-existing documentation or a decision-maker, which are unavailable in this scenario.

allQuestions.text: A patient with massive, un-survivable trauma undergoes prolonged CPR despite no realistic chance of recovery. This scenario best illustrates which ethical concept?
allQuestions.explanation: Medical futility refers to interventions unlikely to produce meaningful benefit, such as prolonged CPR on a patient with un-survivable injuries. Physicians are not ethically obligated to provide futile care, though communicating this to families requires empathy. Beneficence and justice relate to providing benefit and fair resource allocation, not the specific concept of non-beneficial intervention.

allQuestions.text: Which zone of the emergency department is reserved for ESI Level 1 patients such as cardiac arrests and major traumas requiring full team mobilization?
allQuestions.explanation: The Trauma/Resus Bay consists of large, heavily equipped rooms reserved for the most critical ESI Level 1 patients requiring full team mobilization. Fast Track handles minor ESI 4/5 complaints, while the Main ED manages ESI 2–3 patients needing detailed workups. The waiting room and outpatient clinic are not part of acute in-department care.

allQuestions.text: A trauma patient presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and active external hemorrhage. Which type of shock is most consistent with this presentation?
allQuestions.explanation: Active external hemorrhage with hypotension and tachycardia is classic for hypovolemic shock, requiring immediate hemorrhage control and massive transfusion. Cardiogenic and obstructive shock arise from pump or mechanical obstruction problems, not blood loss, while distributive shock stems from vasodilation such as in sepsis. Rapidly diagnosing the shock type is essential to initiate the correct targeted therapy.

allQuestions.text: A patient in a hospital lacking a neurosurgeon requires specialized neurosurgical care not available at that facility. Which disposition option is most appropriate?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Transfer to a specialized facility
allQuestions.explanation: Transfer is indicated when a patient requires specialized care unavailable at the current facility, such as neurosurgery. Admission is appropriate only if the needed resources exist on-site, and discharge home is unsafe for a patient with an unresolved emergent condition. This disposition ensures the patient reaches definitive, appropriate care safely.

allQuestions.text: Hospital-wide bed shortages cause admitted patients to remain in the ED for extended periods. This phenomenon, known as "boarding," most directly compromises which of the four pillars of medical ethics due to the resulting overcrowding and delayed care for new arrivals?
allQuestions.explanation: Boarding creates severe overcrowding that compromises justice by disrupting fair and equitable allocation of ED resources among patients. This systemic issue also directly increases patient mortality.

allQuestions.text: A patient has a documented Do Not Intubate (DNI) order but develops worsening respiratory distress. Which of the following interventions would still be appropriate under this order?
options: Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
originalOptions: Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Non-invasive support such as BiPAP or medications
allQuestions.explanation: A DNI order specifically prohibits placement of a breathing tube, but other treatments such as BiPAP or medications may still be given. Endotracheal intubation, RSI, surgical airway, and mechanical ventilation via ET tube all involve tube placement and are excluded by this order. Distinguishing DNI from DNR is essential, as DNI does not prohibit all supportive care.

allQuestions.text: A patient arrives at the ED with no pulse, no respiratory effort, and obvious signs of death (rigor mortis). To which triage area should this patient be assigned?
allQuestions.explanation: The Black area (or tag) is designated for patients who are deceased or have injuries incompatible with life. Unlike the Red area, which is for salvageable critically ill patients, resources are not directed toward resuscitation of patients already confirmed dead.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents to the ED with a minor laceration requiring simple wound closure, stable vital signs, and no other complaints. Which triage/care pathway is most appropriate?
allQuestions.explanation: Fast Track is designed for low-acuity patients (ESI 4–5) such as those with simple lacerations, minor illnesses, or issues requiring only one or zero resources. This pathway allows for rapid throughput without occupying acute care resources

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best describes the primary goal of resuscitation as one of the three pillars of emergency care?
options: Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
Determining the safest next step for the patient
originalOptions: Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
Determining the safest next step for the patient
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Immediate stabilization of vital signs, taking the highest priority for the EM physician
allQuestions.explanation: Resuscitation is the first and highest priority among the three pillars of emergency care (Resuscitation, Diagnosis, Disposition). Stabilizing the patient's vital signs takes precedence over reaching a definitive diagnosis or determining disposition, since an unstable patient may die before either can occur.

allQuestions.text: A physician determines that continuing CPR on a patient with massive, un-survivable trauma would provide no meaningful benefit. What is this concept called, and what is the physician's ethical obligation?
options: Beneficence; the physician must continue regardless of family wishes
Justice; the physician must involve the ethics committee before any decision
Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care
Autonomy; the family has full authority to demand continued care
Non-maleficence; the physician must transfer the patient immediately
originalOptions: Beneficence; the physician must continue regardless of family wishes
Justice; the physician must involve the ethics committee before any decision
Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care
Autonomy; the family has full authority to demand continued care
Non-maleficence; the physician must transfer the patient immediately
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Medical futility; the physician is not ethically obligated to provide futile care
allQuestions.explanation: Medical futility refers to interventions unlikely to produce meaningful benefit. Physicians are not ethically obligated to provide futile care, though communicating this to a grieving family requires empathy and clear communication, and may involve the ethics committee when conflict arises.

allQuestions.text: A pulseless patient is found in the ED. Bystanders begin CPR immediately while another staff member activates the emergency response. To which triage area does this patient belong?
allQuestions.explanation: Any pulseless patient requires immediate resuscitation and is classified as Red area (ESI Level 1), reflecting the need for immediate, life-saving intervention. This differs from the Black area, which is reserved for patients already confirmed deceased or with injuries incompatible with life.

allQuestions.text: A patient with a new complaint visits her family physician first, who then decides whether specialist referral or hospital admission is needed. This reflects which core principle of Family Medicine?
allQuestions.explanation: First Contact Care means the family physician is typically the initial point of entry into the healthcare system, deciding whether further specialist or hospital care is needed. Continuity, comprehensiveness, and coordination describe ongoing or multi-domain aspects of care rather than this initial gatekeeping role.

allQuestions.text: A physician who has followed the same patient for eight years, reviewing his blood pressure, HbA1c, and personal circumstances at each visit, best demonstrates which principle?
allQuestions.explanation: Continuity of Care refers to a physician remaining consistently involved with a patient over time, building a longitudinal understanding of their condition and life circumstances. While comprehensive and patient-centered care are also relevant to good practice, the defining feature here is the long-term, ongoing relationship.

allQuestions.text: A physician evaluating a patient's knee pain who also reviews her hypertension, vaccination status, and screens for depression is demonstrating which principle?
allQuestions.explanation: Comprehensive Care means addressing all aspects of a patient's health during a single encounter, not just the presenting complaint. Coordination instead refers to organizing care between multiple providers, which is not the focus of this scenario.

allQuestions.text: A physician who reviews a hospital discharge summary, reconciles medications, and arranges follow-up with a cardiologist and endocrinologist is demonstrating which principle?
allQuestions.explanation: Coordination of Care involves organizing a patient's treatment and follow-up across multiple specialists and care settings, as shown by reconciling medications and arranging specialist follow-up. Comprehensive care instead refers to addressing multiple health domains within one visit, not coordinating between providers.

allQuestions.text: Which statement best reflects the concept of patient-centered care as emphasized by Sir William Osler?
options: The great physician treats the disease rather than the patient who has it
The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
The great physician treats only patients who actively request treatment
The good physician treats the patient's family rather than the patient
The great physician avoids exploring the patient's personal ideas and concerns
originalOptions: The great physician treats the disease rather than the patient who has it
The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
The great physician treats only patients who actively request treatment
The good physician treats the patient's family rather than the patient
The great physician avoids exploring the patient's personal ideas and concerns
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The good physician treats the disease, the great physician treats the patient who has the disease
allQuestions.explanation: Osler's quote captures the essence of patient-centered care, distinguishing a good physician who focuses only on disease from a great physician who focuses on the whole patient. The other options invert or distort this principle.

allQuestions.text: A government imposes a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages to reduce future population-wide obesity risk before individuals develop unhealthy habits. This represents which level of prevention?
options: Primary prevention, since it targets an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention, since it detects disease early
Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
Tertiary prevention, since it reduces complications of established disease
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary medical intervention
originalOptions: Primary prevention, since it targets an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention, since it detects disease early
Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
Tertiary prevention, since it reduces complications of established disease
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary medical intervention
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Primordial prevention, since it prevents the emergence of risk factors themselves
allQuestions.explanation: Primordial prevention aims to prevent risk factors from emerging in the first place by shaping healthy social and environmental conditions, such as taxing sugary drinks before unhealthy habits develop. This differs from primary prevention, which controls or eliminates risk factors that already exist.

allQuestions.text: A physician avoids ordering a routine chest x-ray for a patient with a self-limited viral upper respiratory infection, recognizing that further imaging would not change management. This reflects which level of prevention?
allQuestions.explanation: Quaternary prevention involves protecting patients from unnecessary or potentially harmful medical interventions, such as avoiding routine imaging that offers no clinical benefit. This is distinct from primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention, which involve actively intervening on risk factors, disease detection, or complications.

allQuestions.text: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes undergoes an annual retinal examination and foot examination to detect early complications, while his physician also counsels him on medication adherence. Which level of prevention does this scenario best represent?
options: Primary prevention only, since it addresses an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention only, since retinal screening detects asymptomatic disease
Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
Primordial prevention, since it targets social conditions before disease onset
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary intervention
originalOptions: Primary prevention only, since it addresses an existing risk factor
Secondary prevention only, since retinal screening detects asymptomatic disease
Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
Primordial prevention, since it targets social conditions before disease onset
Quaternary prevention, since it avoids unnecessary intervention
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Tertiary prevention, since it aims to prevent complications in a patient with established disease
allQuestions.explanation: Because the patient already has established diabetes, screening for complications such as retinopathy and counseling on adherence falls under tertiary prevention, which aims to reduce complications and disability in patients with existing disease. This is a common exam trap, since annual retinal screening superficially resembles secondary prevention, but the key distinction is that the underlying disease is already present.

allQuestions.text: According to the biopsychosocial model applied in Family Medicine, which combination of domains must a family physician integrate during every consultation?
options: Biological, environmental, and economic factors only
Sociological and biological factors only, excluding psychological factors
originalOptions: Biological, environmental, and economic factors only
Sociological and biological factors only, excluding psychological factors
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Biological, psychological, and sociological factors
allQuestions.explanation: The biopsychosocial model requires family physicians to integrate biological, psychological, and sociological dimensions of a patient's health during every consultation. The distractors substitute unrelated domains or omit one of the three core components.

allQuestions.text: A 62-year-old woman with symptomatic gallstones is informed of the risks and benefits of laparoscopic cholecystectomy by her surgeon. She states she understands the recommendation but declines surgery. The physician documents the discussion, ensures she understands the consequences, and respects her decision while discussing alternative management. Which two ethical principles are most directly demonstrated together in this scenario?
allQuestions.explanation: This scenario demonstrates autonomy through informed refusal, where the patient understands the consequences of declining treatment and the physician documents this understanding as part of informed consent. Justice, confidentiality, and beneficence are not the central principles being tested here, since the scenario centers on the patient's right to make an informed decision about her own care.

allQuestions.text: A 68-year-old man is newly diagnosed with colon cancer after biopsy. He asks his family physician direct questions about his prognosis. The physician answers honestly and compassionately rather than withholding or softening the diagnosis. Which ethical principle is being demonstrated?
allQuestions.explanation: Veracity refers to the physician's duty to tell the patient the truth about their diagnosis and prognosis, even when the news is difficult. Autonomy concerns respecting the patient's right to decide, and confidentiality concerns protecting information, neither of which is the focus here.

allQuestions.text: A 66-year-old man with established chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is enrolled in a pulmonary rehabilitation program and counseled on smoking cessation to slow disease progression and prevent further decline. Which level of prevention does this represent?
allQuestions.explanation: Because the patient already has established COPD, smoking cessation and rehabilitation here aim to reduce complications and disability rather than prevent disease onset, making this tertiary prevention. This differs from primary prevention, where smoking cessation would be used to prevent COPD from developing in the first place.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the "4 Cs" core principles of Family Medicine?
allQuestions.explanation: The "4 Cs" are First Contact, Continuity, Comprehensive, and Coordination of Care, which distinguish Family Medicine from hospital-based specialties. Patient-centered care is an important additional principle in Family Medicine but is not one of the original 4 Cs.

allQuestions.text: A hospital has only one dialysis slot available for multiple patients in need. The care team prioritizes patients using transparent, objective medical criteria rather than social status, connections, or ability to pay. Which ethical principle is most directly demonstrated?
allQuestions.explanation: Justice requires fair and equitable distribution of limited healthcare resources based on objective medical criteria rather than social or financial factors. Beneficence and nonmaleficence relate to benefiting or not harming an individual patient, not to fair allocation across multiple patients.

allQuestions.text: A patient living in a remote village is able to reach basic family medicine services without excessive travel or cost, as the clinic was deliberately placed within reasonable geographic reach of the local population. Which essential attribute of primary care does this best illustrate?
allQuestions.explanation: Accessibility refers to primary care being geographically reachable so that patients, including those in remote areas, can obtain care without excessive burden. Comprehensiveness instead refers to the breadth of services offered, not geographic reach.

allQuestions.text: Death is defined as the complete, irreversible cessation of the integrated function of which three systems?
allQuestions.explanation: Death is defined as complete, irreversible cessation of the integrated function of the central nervous system, respiratory system, and cardiovascular system, reflected by absence of brain stem reflexes. This triad forms the basis for clinically confirming death before postmortem changes even begin.

allQuestions.text: What is the main clinical rationale for recognizing early postmortem changes such as rigor mortis, hypostasis, and decomposition?
options: To determine the exact cause of death immediately
To confirm death and avoid unnecessary resuscitation attempts
To estimate the victim's exact age at death
To identify the weapon used in an assault
To calculate the total blood loss at the scene
originalOptions: To determine the exact cause of death immediately
To confirm death and avoid unnecessary resuscitation attempts
To estimate the victim's exact age at death
To identify the weapon used in an assault
To calculate the total blood loss at the scene
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) To confirm death and avoid unnecessary resuscitation attempts
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: To confirm death and avoid unnecessary resuscitation attempts
allQuestions.explanation: Recognizing these signs confirms that a person is already dead, so there is no need to perform CPR, defibrillation, or give adrenaline, saving time and effort. It also has a social value, since attempting resuscitation on an obviously dead body in front of family can be inappropriate.

allQuestions.text: The pale areas seen at pressure points within a region of postmortem hypostasis are best explained by:
options: Increased hemoglobin breakdown at those sites
Localized rigor mortis affecting the skin
Blood being unable to accumulate due to compression at those points
Early putrefaction changes at contact points
Reduced carboxyhemoglobin formation at those areas
originalOptions: Increased hemoglobin breakdown at those sites
Localized rigor mortis affecting the skin
Blood being unable to accumulate due to compression at those points
Early putrefaction changes at contact points
Reduced carboxyhemoglobin formation at those areas
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Blood being unable to accumulate due to compression at those points
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Blood being unable to accumulate due to compression at those points
allQuestions.explanation: This phenomenon, called pressure pallor, occurs because pressure at contact points squeezes blood out and prevents it from stagnating there, unlike the surrounding dependent skin. It is a useful clue for reconstructing the body's position or contact surfaces after death.

allQuestions.text: Rigor mortis characteristically begins first in which muscle group before descending through the body?
options: Muscles of the hands and fingers
Small muscles of the face and jaw
originalOptions: Muscles of the hands and fingers
Small muscles of the face and jaw
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Small muscles of the face and jaw
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Small muscles of the face and jaw
allQuestions.explanation: Rigor mortis typically starts in the small muscles of the face and jaw before progressing downward through the body. Because it preserves the position at the time of death, its distribution can help reconstruct how the body was positioned when the person died.

allQuestions.text: A body found suspended by a ligature around the neck, with compression caused by the weight of the body, is most consistent with which manner of death?
allQuestions.explanation: Hanging is compression of the neck by the weight of the body (or part of it) and is mostly suicidal, though it can occasionally be accidental. This contrasts with strangulation by ligature or hands, which is mostly homicidal.

allQuestions.text: Choking, as a mechanical anoxic death, results from occlusion of the respiratory passages at which level?
options: Nose and mouth level, from outside
Chest and abdomen level, by external force
originalOptions: Nose and mouth level, from outside
Chest and abdomen level, by external force
allQuestions.explanation: Choking is the mechanical anoxic death caused by occlusion of the respiratory passages from inside, at the level of the larynx, such as by a swallowed foreign object. This distinguishes it from smothering (mouth/nose, external) and traumatic asphyxia (chest/abdomen).

allQuestions.text: The presence of froth at the mouth when a body is retrieved from water is most suggestive of:
options: Death from traumatic asphyxia before submersion
originalOptions: Death from traumatic asphyxia before submersion
allQuestions.explanation: If froth is found coming from the mouth when the body is pulled from the water, this indicates the person was still alive and breathing when submerged, i.e., antemortem drowning. This distinction is forensically essential to determine whether the person fell into water before or after death.

allQuestions.text: In a burn victim, a blood carboxyhemoglobin (CO) level above approximately 10% suggests which of the following?
options: The person died before the fire started
The person had chronic COPD prior to death
The person was alive during the fire (antemortem burning)
The fire was electrical rather than chemical in origin
The body was moved into the fire after death
originalOptions: The person died before the fire started
The person had chronic COPD prior to death
The person was alive during the fire (antemortem burning)
The fire was electrical rather than chemical in origin
The body was moved into the fire after death
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The person was alive during the fire (antemortem burning)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The person was alive during the fire (antemortem burning)
allQuestions.explanation: A COHb level above roughly 10% indicates the person was breathing combustion smoke and therefore alive during the fire, confirming antemortem burning. This is analogous to using froth to confirm antemortem drowning, both distinguishing whether the person was alive at the time of the fatal event.

allQuestions.text: "Gagging" differs from "smothering" mainly in that gagging involves closure of the airway:
options: At the neck level rather than the mouth
By a ligature rather than by hands
At the chest level rather than the mouth
From inside the mouth rather than from outside
Due to natural disease rather than external force
originalOptions: At the neck level rather than the mouth
By a ligature rather than by hands
At the chest level rather than the mouth
From inside the mouth rather than from outside
Due to natural disease rather than external force
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) From inside the mouth rather than from outside
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: From inside the mouth rather than from outside
allQuestions.explanation: Gagging resembles smothering but occurs from inside, such as when a piece of cloth (the gag) is pushed into the mouth and pressed backward, closing the mouth and nose internally rather than externally. Both act at the same anatomical level (mouth and nose) but differ in the direction/source of occlusion.

allQuestions.text: Which wound feature at the wound bottom is most useful in distinguishing a laceration from an incised (cut) wound?
allQuestions.explanation: Lacerations, caused by blunt trauma, typically show tissue bridging at the wound bottom because some tougher tissue strands resist tearing, along with irregular edges and contused margins. Incised wounds, from sharp objects, characteristically lack bridging and instead show regular edges with a clean, clear margin.

allQuestions.text: A patient underwent uncomplicated cataract surgery three weeks ago and now presents with a red, painful eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A patient with recent cataract surgery presenting with red, painful eye must be assumed to have endophthalmitis until proven otherwise, as it is a sight-threatening postoperative infection requiring urgent management. Allergic conjunctivitis and blepharitis do not carry this same post-surgical urgency.

allQuestions.text: During the swinging light test, light is moved to the affected eye and both pupils dilate instead of constricting. What does this finding represent?
options: A positive relative afferent pupillary defect
originalOptions: A positive relative afferent pupillary defect
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) A positive relative afferent pupillary defect
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A positive relative afferent pupillary defect
allQuestions.explanation: A positive RAPD occurs when light swung to the affected eye produces paradoxical dilation of both pupils because that eye has a reduced afferent signal reaching the brain. This paradoxical response distinguishes RAPD from a normal reflex, where both pupils would constrict equally.

allQuestions.text: A glaucoma patient with a known sulfa allergy needs additional intraocular pressure control. Which medication should be avoided?
allQuestions.explanation: Acetazolamide is a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, so it must be avoided in patients with a documented sulfa allergy. The other listed glaucoma agents belong to different drug classes and do not carry this cross-reactivity risk.

allQuestions.text: A patient has limited abduction of one eye on examination, with normal movement in all other directions. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated limitation of abduction in one eye reflects lateral rectus weakness, which is supplied by the abducent (CN VI) nerve. The oculomotor and trochlear nerves control other extraocular muscles and would not cause this isolated abduction deficit.

allQuestions.text: A patient on long-term antimalarial therapy develops progressive visual field loss. Which drug is most associated with this retinal complication?
allQuestions.explanation: Chloroquine and related antimalarials are well recognized to cause retinal toxicity with long-term use, which can lead to progressive visual field loss. Roaccutane instead causes severe ocular dryness, and topical steroids are more associated with cataract and raised intraocular pressure.

allQuestions.text: On confrontation visual field testing, the examiner notes the patient's blind spot is larger than expected. What should this finding raise suspicion for?
options: Optic nerve disorder such as papilledema
originalOptions: Optic nerve disorder such as papilledema
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Optic nerve disorder such as papilledema
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Optic nerve disorder such as papilledema
allQuestions.explanation: The physiological blind spot should have a fixed, unenlarged size on confrontation testing; enlargement points toward an optic nerve disorder such as papilledema or optic neuritis. A refractive error or cataract would not selectively enlarge the blind spot.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with bilateral limitation of abduction on eye movement examination. Which location is most likely responsible?
allQuestions.explanation: Bilateral limitation of abduction suggests a lesion affecting both abducent nerve pathways simultaneously, which localizes to the brainstem rather than a single peripheral nerve. Chiasmal or occipital lesions instead produce visual field defects rather than isolated bilateral eye movement restriction.

allQuestions.text: A patient with a history of chronic topical steroid use for ocular inflammation develops gradually worsening vision. Which type of cataract is most classically associated with steroid use?
allQuestions.explanation: Chronic steroid use is classically linked to posterior subcapsular cataract formation, which characteristically causes early visual disturbance despite a relatively clear lens periphery. Nuclear sclerotic and cortical cataracts are more typically age-related rather than steroid-induced.

allQuestions.text: During ophthalmoscopy, the examiner needs to determine whether the fundus image belongs to the right or left eye. Which anatomical relationship allows this distinction?
options: Position of the optic disc relative to the fovea
Position of the optic disc relative to the macula
originalOptions: Position of the optic disc relative to the fovea
Position of the optic disc relative to the macula
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Position of the optic disc relative to the macula
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Position of the optic disc relative to the macula
allQuestions.explanation: The optic disc lies nasal to the macula, so identifying which side the disc appears on relative to the macula tells the examiner whether the image is of the right or left eye. Vessel size and choroidal color do not vary in a way that reliably indicates laterality.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with progressive loss of the outer visual field in both eyes, sparing the central visual field. Which underlying process is most likely responsible?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Compression at the optic chiasm
allQuestions.explanation: Bitemporal visual field loss reflects damage to the crossing nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm, most commonly from a compressive lesion such as a pituitary adenoma. Retinal detachment and AMD instead produce peripheral or central field loss localized to one eye rather than a bitemporal pattern.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best defines psychiatry as a medical specialty?
options: A subspecialty of neurology focused on brain imaging
The branch of medicine concerned with prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of mental disorders
A field limited to prescribing medication for behavioral complaints
A discipline concerned only with social counseling services
A field limited to managing psychotic disorders in hospitals
originalOptions: A subspecialty of neurology focused on brain imaging
The branch of medicine concerned with prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of mental disorders
A field limited to prescribing medication for behavioral complaints
A discipline concerned only with social counseling services
A field limited to managing psychotic disorders in hospitals
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The branch of medicine concerned with prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of mental disorders
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The branch of medicine concerned with prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of mental disorders
allQuestions.explanation: Psychiatry is defined by its four core functions: prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation. Because psychiatrists are physicians, they integrate biological, psychological, and social factors rather than being limited to medication or counseling alone.

allQuestions.text: Why is psychiatry considered clinically important according to the lecture?
options: It only becomes relevant during inpatient hospital stays
It is exclusively concerned with rare genetic brain disorders
Mental illness increases mortality from physical disease
It has no measurable effect on outcomes in physical illness
It is relevant mainly to forensic and legal settings
originalOptions: It only becomes relevant during inpatient hospital stays
It is exclusively concerned with rare genetic brain disorders
Mental illness increases mortality from physical disease
It has no measurable effect on outcomes in physical illness
It is relevant mainly to forensic and legal settings
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Mental illness increases mortality from physical disease
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Mental illness increases mortality from physical disease
allQuestions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes that roughly 1 in 8 people worldwide are affected by mental disorders, depression is the second leading cause of disability after cardiovascular disease, and mental illness worsens outcomes in physical disease, underscoring why every physician practices some psychiatry.

allQuestions.text: According to the biopsychosocial model, mental illness is best understood as:
options: A condition with a single dominant biological cause
A purely psychological phenomenon unrelated to biology
A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
A social construct with no biological basis
A condition determined solely by genetics
originalOptions: A condition with a single dominant biological cause
A purely psychological phenomenon unrelated to biology
A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
A social construct with no biological basis
A condition determined solely by genetics
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A result of interaction between biological, psychological, and social domains
allQuestions.explanation: The biopsychosocial model frames mental illness as multifactorial, arising from the interaction of biological factors (genetics, brain function, neurotransmitters), psychological factors (personality, coping, trauma), and social factors (family, culture, employment).

allQuestions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes mental health from mental illness?
options: Mental health is the complete absence of any disorder
Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
Mental illness and mental health cannot coexist
Mental health refers only to absence of psychotic symptoms
Mental health is determined by occupational performance alone
originalOptions: Mental health is the complete absence of any disorder
Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
Mental illness and mental health cannot coexist
Mental health refers only to absence of psychotic symptoms
Mental health is determined by occupational performance alone
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Mental health includes emotional well-being and social functioning
allQuestions.explanation: The lecture explicitly states mental health is not merely the absence of disease; it is a positive state encompassing emotional well-being, psychological resilience, social functioning, occupational ability, and stress coping.

allQuestions.text: For a condition to be classified as a mental disorder, which combination of features must generally be present?
options: Disturbance in cognition or behavior, with no distress required
Any unusual thought, regardless of its effect on functioning
Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
A diagnosis made only after psychiatric hospitalization
originalOptions: Disturbance in cognition or behavior, with no distress required
Any unusual thought, regardless of its effect on functioning
Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
A diagnosis made only after psychiatric hospitalization
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Disturbance in a core domain plus significant distress or impairment
allQuestions.explanation: A mental disorder requires both a disturbance in one of the core domains (cognition, emotion, behavior, interpersonal functioning) AND that this disturbance produces significant distress or impairment affecting social life, relationships, work, or studying.

allQuestions.text: A patient describes an anxiety symptom in which the world suddenly feels vivid, "like a rainbow," yet the sensation is distressing and overwhelming rather than pleasant. This is most consistent with which symptom?
options: Fear, with the world perceived as uniformly dark
Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
Elation, as a pure mood symptom without anxiety
originalOptions: Fear, with the world perceived as uniformly dark
Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
Elation, as a pure mood symptom without anxiety
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Panic, which can present as a heightened, vivid perception of reality
allQuestions.explanation: The lecture notes panic can sometimes present as a vivid, almost euphoric perception of the world (colorful, "life feels great") rather than only the classic dark, threatening perception seen in fear, making panic recognizable in atypical presentations.

allQuestions.text: Hallucinations and delusions are classified under which domains of the Mental Status Examination, respectively?
allQuestions.explanation: Hallucinations (perceiving things that are not present) fall under perception, while delusions (fixed false beliefs) fall under thought content. The lecture separates these domains within the MSE, alongside thought process, cognition, insight, and judgment.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is emphasized as essential to always assess as part of psychiatric risk assessment?
options: Only suicide risk, addressed separately from other risks
Only substance use, as the most common comorbidity
Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
Only homicidal ideation in forensic patients
Only domestic violence in female patients
originalOptions: Only suicide risk, addressed separately from other risks
Only substance use, as the most common comorbidity
Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
Only homicidal ideation in forensic patients
Only domestic violence in female patients
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Suicide, self-harm, homicidal thoughts, psychosis, and abuse
allQuestions.explanation: Risk assessment is part of every psychiatric evaluation and must always cover this full set of areas, since each carries potentially serious and preventable consequences if missed during assessment.

allQuestions.text: Which pairing correctly identifies the brain stimulation therapies discussed among treatment modalities?
allQuestions.explanation: The lecture lists brain stimulation therapies as a distinct treatment modality alongside psychotherapy and medication, specifically naming ECT (Electroconvulsive Therapy) and TMS (Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation).

allQuestions.text: According to the lecture, stigma in psychiatry manifests in three primary forms. Which set correctly represents these?
options: Structural, familial, and public stigma only
originalOptions: Structural, familial, and public stigma only
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Public, self, and structural stigma
allQuestions.explanation: Stigma manifests as public stigma (societal discrimination and stereotypes), self-stigma (internalizing negative views leading to shame), and structural stigma (institutional policies limiting rights or care), together contributing to delayed treatment and poor adherence.

allQuestions.text: On CT, an acute intracranial hemorrhage (0–3 days old) typically appears as which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: Fresh blood is denser than brain parenchyma, so acute hemorrhage (0–3 days) appears hyperdense on CT. This density evolves predictably over time, becoming isodense in the subacute phase and hypodense once chronic.

allQuestions.text: A hemorrhage older than 4 weeks (chronic stage) typically appears on CT as which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: As clot breaks down and fluid content increases, hemorrhage density decreases over time: hyperdense when acute, isodense when subacute, and hypodense once chronic (over 4 weeks). Confusing the acute and chronic stages is a common exam trap since the pattern is opposite to what students expect.

allQuestions.text: Which early CT finding is characteristic of hyperacute ischemic stroke (6–24 hours)?
allQuestions.explanation: In the early hyperacute phase of ischemia, cytotoxic edema causes cortical hypodensity with loss of grey-white matter differentiation and gyral effacement. This is an early, subtle sign, while volume loss and calcification only appear in the chronic stage.

allQuestions.text: Vasogenic edema on brain imaging is classically seen surrounding which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: Vasogenic edema classically surrounds tumors, abscesses, and hemorrhages due to disruption of the blood-brain barrier. This is distinct from cytotoxic edema, which occurs in ischemia and affects both grey and white matter directly.

allQuestions.text: Which radiological feature helps distinguish pulmonary consolidation from lobar collapse?
allQuestions.explanation: Consolidation shows airspace opacification with air bronchograms and no volume loss or fissure displacement, since the airways remain patent. Collapse, in contrast, shows volume loss and fissure displacement toward the affected lobe, with no air bronchograms.

allQuestions.text: Which imaging modality is preferred for diagnosing acute cholecystitis?
allQuestions.explanation: Ultrasound is the preferred modality for cholecystitis, showing a distended gallbladder, thickened wall, calculi, and pericholecystic fluid. It is also the preferred first study for bowel obstruction and appendicitis per the lecture.

allQuestions.text: In a patient with suspected bowel perforation, which radiograph is most sensitive for detecting free intraperitoneal air?
allQuestions.explanation: An erect chest x-ray is the most sensitive plain radiograph for detecting free intraperitoneal gas, appearing as lucent air beneath the diaphragm. Abdominal signs such as the Rigler (double wall) sign and football sign are also associated findings of pneumoperitoneum.

allQuestions.text: A barium enema shows an "apple core" sign with eccentric wall thickening in the descending colon. This finding is characteristic of which condition?
allQuestions.explanation: The apple core sign reflects eccentric, annular wall thickening typical of colorectal carcinoma and is often associated with luminal obstruction. This classic contrast-study sign was specifically highlighted in the lecture for colorectal cancer.

allQuestions.text: What is the earliest radiological finding in ankylosing spondylitis?
